(1866-1900) Docility and love for the Vicar of Christ — Respect for priests and men religious — An unachieved project: the Sons of St. Anne — Misunderstandings within the Institute — Apostolic Visitation — Denouncement to the Holy Office of the Book: “Travagli e conforti dell’anima nel cammino della perfezione” — Outcome of the Apostolic Visitation and the Mother’s rectitude acknowledged.

Docility and love for the Vicar of Christ ~ The words of the Gospel describing Jesus’ relationship with those who are faithful to him are always moving, also when they have the solemnity of true messianic claims: “I am the good shepherd; I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep…. They too will listen to my voice, and there will be only one flock and one shepherd” (Jn 10:14-16).

This “listening” is followed by the reliable and necessary sign of the holiness and authenticity of every undertaking. Those who do not know Christ or have no profound experience of him, who do not distinguish the voice as that of their own Vicar and follow him with compliance, are not of the fold; consequently they are not builders of God’s kingdom, and those who do not build with Christ in his Church accumulate ruins.

Rosa Gattorno is presented to us as a faithful and tender disciple of Christ from the very beginning of her important undertaking; she founded her work through obedience to Pius IX, she wanted it to be entirely in the Pope’s hands and guided it with the most filial docility to the Vicar of Christ. How deep Mother Rosa’s love for the Pope was! We find a lasting sign of it in the Rule given to her religious: “The Daughters of St. Anne must first of all be deeply convinced that the words of Jesus Christ are infallible and that by conforming their deeds to them, in heaven they will succeed in seeing Jesus Christ himself, who is the eternal and infinite truth. They should ask for the grace to be ever fully united to the infallible head of the Church, the Supreme Pontiff from whom the teaching of Jesus Christ is always received. They must also seek in God and in his grace, that source of living water which can make them eternally blessed”.1

This Rule, which remains fundamental in the history of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, was wholeheartedly lived by Mother Rosa. Her filial, absolute union with the Holy See is documented by many episodes already recounted, more of which will be told in these pages; among them some are very familiar, such as the symbolic gifts which she liked to present to Pope Pius IX when she was received by him in audience.

In addition to important spiritual help, the Mother had in exchange from that great Pope as many proofs of fatherly confidence and undoubted fondness, as when he offered her some magnificent pears. But filial union with the Pope was manifested in Rosa Gattorno in difficult times, when it was not merely a matter of affectionate homage but of generous obedience concerning what affected her and the work she had founded; we explained this with regard to the drafting of the Rule and the Institute’s definitive approval. In the informative processes, on this topic we read the valuable deposition of an eminent figure: “The Bishop of Piacenza gave the most flattering praise of the Servant of God to the Sacred Congregation […], in applauding her virtues, he highlighted Rosa Gattorno’s prompt and generous obedience in her endeavor to comply with the orders of the Holy See”.2

Respect for priests and men religious ~ It should nevertheless be noted that in her role as Superior General, Mother Rosa always treated ministers of God, even of the humblest rank, with special respect. No one will be surprised that various ecclesiastics created difficulties for the Mother’s work or in different ways were the cause of certain troubles; the limitations of the human mind ensure that it is very difficult to fully grasp and esteem the thinking of others as one ought, and this gives rise to misunderstandings and contradictions. However, in these clashes the Mother would first of all resort to prayer, she was docile to the superior authority on which she depended, and her maxim was never to make known to others anything that might damage the reputation of the ecclesiastics themselves.3

In the many houses of the Institute that were scattered in the different dioceses, these priests and prelates would often converse with some of the sisters, whom they believed more easily than they should and by whom they were so influenced as not to think much of the Mother General: that is, they thought and said that she was rather stubborn in her way of governing and also very personal. However, they later confessed that with a dispassionate appraisal, it was clear that this form of governance was due instead to her vast knowledge of the facts and persons of the Institute.4

But this did not prevent the Foundress from having to face very serious dilemmas and difficulties given, precisely, her delicacy in never wishing to oppose ecclesiastics.

Other facts can be deduced from her voluminous correspondence with the distant superiors who sometimes complained of some priest who was disturbing the peace and discipline of the religious house; in all these situations never a word of condemnation concerning those priests escaped the lips or pen of Mother Gattorno. Only when the facts were evident, would she write: “What is to be done? You must pray, pray a lot!”. She never mentioned those priests in her answers, indeed, by extension, she never wrote the word “priest”, but at most was satisfied with the simple letter “p”, to avoid any risk of slandering ecclesiastics.

This veneration which she demonstrated and inferred in her dealings with priests, was even more pronounced when it came to bishops. Sr. Anna Nestore Tagliabue assures us that in her conferences to the religious she not only urged them to show respect, but real obedience to their ecclesiastical superiors. She recommended to the superiors of other houses that they depend on the local bishops and accept their opinions and advice in matters of their competence.

Another Daughter of St. Anne candidly confesses: “At times, when some measure of the local bishop did not seem right to us sisters, the Servant of God would want obedience without discussion and said that superiors should always be obeyed; that if they make mistakes it is they who are responsible”.5

Before taking decisions in the governance of the Institute and especially in the most difficult circumstances, she would redouble her penance and prayers and also have her religious say many prayers. From her letters one sees how constant she was in recourse to and trust in Jesus Christ and St. Anne: she often drew such enlightenment from this faith that she felt surer than ever in deciding what to do. Yet if she was opposed by bishops or other ecclesiastical authorities she would express her observations and, if they insisted, obey their judgment. After a while, however, these ecclesiastics would have to admit their own error, and return to what the Mother had previously thought. Various figures, even of high rank, pointed out this attitude in Rosa Gattorno, admiring her obedience and respect which are indeed all the truer and greater when they involve surrendering a clear and upright opinion of one’s own.

In the second half of the 19th century, when Rosa Gattorno founded her Institute and many similar ones dedicated to apostolic life were flourishing, numerous points were left to the prudence of the superiors general; thus there was great leeway in arranging the novitiate period, in admittance to the vows, in the elections of superiors, in the opening of new houses. In all this, Mother Rosa followed the accepted customs and instructions given to her by authoritative religious such as Fr. Bernardino da Portogruaro, Minister General of the Friars Minor.

Then as the Holy See gradually issued instructions, she wanted everyone to put them faithfully into practice, and allowed no complaints. She never had anything to change concerning the authority/obedience relationship with regard to revealing her own conscience to the superiors, since she had not introduced this usage in her Institute.

A rather regrettable incident had occurred in an American house and the superior seemed almost glad that a sister should be involved in a bitter disagreement with her confessor. The Mother, as soon as she heard about it, answered in these terms: “Now there is one thing: I hear that Sr. Anna Raffaela is being maltreated by her confessor. Well, even [if] she might have deserved it, a sister should not be driven to desperation. Take her to someone else for confession, but rescue her! Be careful, you could have a big problem, do you realize? I warn you that we are responsible before God; if you do not want her, send her wherever you think best, but do not let her despair. We do so much to gain souls, and then should those in our own care be lost? For pity’s sake, be careful!”.6 She returns in heartfelt tones to the same subject two months later: “the matter of the sister troubles me greatly: for pity’s sake, be careful!”.7

She herself knew by experience how a soul can suffer in delicate sacramental communications. She had a special veneration for her confessors and for her spiritual directors, although she did not always receive satisfactory answers from them to her queries concerning communications received from the Lord; therefore her spirit continued to be in anguish. However, the Mother accepted all this as a test and it did not weaken her sentiment of veneration for her director.8

She did not claim that all the sisters had the same strength of mind; on the contrary, in accordance with the spirit of the Church, she wanted all human weakness to be taken into account and did not worry about any minor shortcomings which could derive from this discipline, because certain sisters had their own understanding of the support of the confessors granted to them by the Church.9 She only sought to find a remedy for them with all tact and prudence.

An unachieved project: the Sons of St. Anne ~ Mother Rosa suggested choosing as confessors preferably religious priests living in communities, or friars;10 and since these were not always easily available, she nurtured the idea of founding an Institute of priests parallel to the sisters and in line with the inspiration she had received earlier: “I always have before me the three drops of blood which are meant to be the three orders. I had never thought of Sons of St. Anne, but believed there should be a branch of the Daughters of St. Anne of the contemplative life, cloistered…” (M. 5.1, p.91). Mother Rosa’s secret aspiration was once again reinforced by divine intervention. She affirms in her Memorie: “I always [feel] a strong impulse to do my utmost to found the Sons of St. Anne. My God, how should I set about it? I was thinking along these lines because I cannot find the draft of the Rule I had and which was inspired in me by my Good; I know I gave it to the Father but it can’t be found. So is this loss supposed to be evidence that the [Sons] of St. Anne are not meant to be founded? […] Everything is established by my Good, and I already see the Sons of the heart of the Saint all intent and filled with love of God, working for his glory, converting sinners, evangelizing the whole world and giving the work of the Daughters a most beautiful luster. Oh, blessed dream!” (M. 7, 21; 24).

Thus the Mother had her eye on various priests of excellent spirit, who were already looking after and affectionately involved in her Institute. Her first attempt was with Fr. Giovanni Boffetti, parish priest of Vespolate, Novara, in 1874. The scarcity of the documentation does not enable us to determine what initial steps were actually taken, but in 1875 the project was sufficiently mature; however, it never came to fruition.11 In the Memorie we find various references, especially around 1882, which predict that the project might not be implemented, and yet do not enable us to identify the person whom Mother Rosa felt was chosen by God for this purpose (cf. M. 5.1, pp. 89-93).12

Another more clearly described attempt, although destined to failure as were the previous ones, was that of Fr. Granito di Belmonte.13

One passage in the Memorie seems to refer in particular to this person: “How my Good is preparing for the Sons of St. Anne is something great and extraordinary. I saw what happened in a person who was to be the one to have helped me but he is not generous [in responding] to the call and is afraid; so he will do [something] but not everything. What fear does!” (M. 5.4, p.7).

On 6 December 1886, during a private audience with Pope Leo XIII, Fr. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte explained the project of the foundation of the Sons of St. Anne to the Pontiff. He was asked to set down his intentions and the purpose of the new Institute in writing; he did so on 8 December, and gave the letter to Mgr. Nazareno Marzolini.14 Advised by the Pope to found the work in his native diocese, Fr. Di Belmonte made the plan known to the archbishop on 6 January 1887.15 Cardinal Sanfelice, obviously of a different opinion, sent the following rescript: “Having considered the matter carefully, as the work has been proposed (at least to us), we declare or rather we feel that it is not expedient”.16 Fr. di Belmonte did not surrender his weapons. The following year, on 26 August 1888, seeking to circumvent the obstacle, he presented together with another four Neapolitan priests, the request for approval of the “Devoted league of Priests” which was intended to serve the spiritual good of the Daughters of St. Anne. Cardinal Sanfelice approved and generously blessed the project on 28 August 1888.

When Mother Rosa was informed of the steps already taken, fearing disorder in the Institute, her reaction was unexpectedly lively.17

She informed the Cardinal Protector who immediately asked Fr. Granito di Belmonte for explanations. Despite the exchange of letters which shed light on the effective intentions of these priests and on the positive quality of their project, it was definitively discarded.18

Misunderstandings within the Institute ~ Mother Rosa had such goings on in her houses at that time that she can be justified for having entertained that idea. There had been no lack of priests in America who even took the liberty of changing the way of making religious profession in the Institute, casting serious doubts on its validity.19

In the meantime, the Mother was doing all she could to ensure that the assistance of priests was effective for her religious, and was most ingenious in atoning for certain errors of others without damaging the esteem due to the priest. One preacher, during the community retreat, permitted himself to make numerous unwise insinuations, saying for example, that the superiors were very partial to vocations from noble families and that they were therefore over tolerant about the other prerequisites for religious life; furthermore, he praised freedom in dealing with the ecclesiastical superiors, and urged the sisters to have recourse to the Roman Congregations against the superiors. He returned several times to such topics in his preaching, which ended by fomenting dissipation rather than reflection, and suspicion of the legitimate authority rather than religious obedience. Mother Rosa, without making any remarks in the presence of the religious, limited herself to advising Cardinal Verga of the matter and for the duration of that retreat dispensed the community from silence so that they would not dwell on the preacher’s strange suggestions.20

A superior of Bolivia, recalled to Italy, had planned with a priest to hide a substantial sum of money which she should have sent to the Generalate long before. Instead she wanted to keep it to use it in her own way for the Institute when she returned to Bolivia, as she hoped. This sort of thing perhaps occurred more frequently in that remote land where some of the clergy readily indulged the good faith and ignorance of the Rule which in some religious were accompanied by zeal to extend the Institute. But the Mother, already suspicious, investigated the strange administrative irregularity patiently and discreetly, and finally managed to make the sister, who had already returned to Italy, confess her misdemeanor. Everything was patched up as well as possible, but the name of the priest who had actually been remiss remained shrouded in the most discreet silence.21

Such incidents must have disgusted some people who thought the Mother authoritarian and excessively rigid, while in fact her sense of responsibility and great fidelity to her task were evident. She wanted not only piety and apostolic zeal but obedience and poverty, which are the basis of religious life; to have permitted any relaxation of this would have been to betray the mandate entrusted to her by the Church. Therefore she was wont to say and write that in the houses where poverty was well observed, a religious spirit and observance in every other point also existed; likewise, nothing would be lacking for their honest maintenance. However, wherever poverty was in some way tarnished, there would be many gaping wounds in their religious soul.22

Those who are expert in the state of consecration to God, will easily agree in admitting the truth of this maxim; moreover, St. Ignatius also called poverty the “solid wall” of religion, and wanted it to be lovingly cherished, as mother, in every dimension of his order.

In fact, Gospel poverty makes room for fuller trust in the Lord and for dedication in proclaiming the kingdom.

Nonetheless, here and there, some superiors wished to use their talent for savings made in the local administration or in the donations they had received. Although they were intended for some beautiful work which they thought would result in the glory of God, Mother Gattorno, who submissively followed the measures of the Holy See, would call them to order and refer to the prohibitions of the Sacred Congregation for Bishops and Regulars;23 savings were to be sent to the Generalate, since the Institute, on the basis of its Constitutions, had a central administration.

Apostolic Visitation ~ We have wished to mention this specific point because a difficulty, indeed a harsh cross for the Mother, arose precisely from this Visitation. Certain superiors, but not many, interpreted the directives of the central government strangely, indeed in open opposition to them they undertook to increase their savings at any cost with the ambition of sending larger sums to the Generalate, thereby arbitrarily depriving the sisters of what the Institute normally gave to them all, and causing them considerable suffering. Complaints were made and were followed by protests. The Mother came to hear of at least some of them; she immediately reprimanded severely the superiors who were behaving in this way, but in many houses the disorder continued so that certain discontented religious were motivated to have direct recourse to the Sacred Congregation for Bishops and Regulars. This led to an Apostolic Visitation.24

Before proceeding to treat this event, we would like to answer a question which has certainly arisen in the minds of readers. How could Mother Rosa have had superiors of this kind? Aren’t these episodes a sign that their protagonists were inadequately formed? Were the communities therefore entrusted to incapable persons? We are answered by a letter from the Mother herself to Sr. Anna Virginia Gaggi, who was complaining precisely of having been sent a difficult sister from Rome. “You say to me, why send Sr. Anna Andreina who is proud and does not want to obey; that we knew what she was like and ought not to have sent her. My God, can it be that we knew? No! […]. A discerning spirit [of hearts] would have been needed; but far from having one, I am a poor wretched creature in everything […]. Therefore, humanly speaking, [the sister] was good and full of good will here, but we also know that human beings are more changeable than the weather”.25

In fact the Mother took great care to form the superiors, teaching them wisdom and inculcating in them the fundamental principles of charity and prudence; she appointed some who had not much experience of religious life, but whom she had sufficiently tested; it was not usually these who caused her to regret,26 but others, who let themselves be swept away by a worldly mentality and, wanting to act as their talents prompted them, forgot to be pure instruments of God.

Returning to the Apostolic Visitation, it should be noted that this was the only official one the Institute had. The first intervention of the ecclesiastical authorities in 1890, as has been said, was unofficial.

Instead, the second was far more important and was entrusted in 1898 by Cardinal Isidoro Verga to Dom Domenico Serafini, then Abbot General of the Benedictines of Subiaco, who later became Bishop of Spoleto (1900) after the death of Rosa Gattorno, Assessor of the Holy Office (1911) and finally Cardinal, on 28 May 1914. The precise goal of this most delicate task given to such an authoritative figure, was to “remedy the disturbances that existed in the Institute”, as Cardinal Verga said, who was its Protector and also Prefect of the Sacred Congregation for Bishops and Regulars.

Denouncement to the Holy Office of the Book: “Travagli e conforti dell’anima nel cammino della perfezione” ~ One of the difficulties that required an intervention of this kind was the publication of the book written by Mother Rosa, Travagli e conforti dell’anima nel cammino della perfezione, which the Princess Emilia di Fitalia had had printed.27 The book, which told the history of the Institute in allegorical form might have given rise to erroneous interpretations but there were no doctrinal or moral grounds for its condemnation. However, an initial denouncement of it by the Redemptorist, Fr. Ernesto Bresciani, reached the Holy Office (17 January 1898); he judged the writing simply “boring”, but also possibly damaging for the sisters to whom it had been distributed.

The Apostolic Visitor’s first act was therefore to withdraw all existing copies.

Years earlier, in about 1890, Fr. Serafini had been at the monastery of San Giuliano in Genoa and had met Rosa Gattorno’s sister-in-law, Amalia Custo, who as we have seen, was exceedingly hostile to her. When Fr. Serafini was leaving for Rome, he received the first news of Mother Rosa from her, with these bitter words: “You are now going to Rome: there is a certain Rosa Gattorno there who makes believe she is a saint and deceives everyone; try to make the scales fall from the eyes of the mystified”.28

These blatantly hostile words were soon forgotten, but the Benedictine remembered them when he was appointed Visitor.

Fr. Domenico Serafini, on hearing that Mother Rosa was at the Mother House in Piacenza, decided to go and see her in that city to notify her of his office and to begin the visitation. He arrived with his own brother, then Abbot of San Giovanni in Parma. The Mother came down to meet the two Abbots in the parlor, accompanied by her two assistants, Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega and Sr. Anna M. Teresa Patti di Sorrentino and presented them, recalling their illustrious families, perhaps to have them better recognized and to highlight the virtues of the renunciation in which they were serving God. After the first civilities, Fr. Serafini explained his purpose and presented his credentials. When she had read the document, surprised and pained, Mother Rosa said: “Yes, I know that I am good for nothing, that I ruin everything: I therefore resign from this moment…”. She could not go on and had to leave the room to give vent to her tears. We cannot doubt her sincerity in speaking of herself in this way, since she had frequently written and spoken in the same vein to her sisters and had even insisted on being stripped of her office as Mother General.29

The decree of Apostolic Visitation was a clear sign of some disorder in the Institute; in any case, she sincerely wanted to give a free hand to the Holy See’s envoy, renouncing all her offices and gladly submitting to total obedience.

But the Visitor reassured her immediately as the circumstance required: there was absolutely no question of her resignation; he had not come to destroy God’s work, but only to become acquainted with it, to clarify individual situations and refer them to the ecclesiastical authority; if he were to find something that needed correction, he would do it with her and he would be of help to her; lastly, he would depend on the Holy See’s measures. They then made arrangements to begin hearing the religious the following day.

That visitation continued for about five years, thus ending three years after Mother Gattorno’s death: the measures taken were communicated to her successor in the governance of the Institute and were unimportant. Here it is interesting above all to follow Mother Rosa’s conduct in those serious circumstances, and in so doing we would like to draw from sources above all suspicion.

She first of all refrained from giving any instructions to her religious on how to behave or speak to the Visitor, and indeed she forbade her secretaries and superiors to do anything of the kind,30 thus leaving them all the greatest freedom to speak as they saw fit. In no way or for any reason or pretext did she impede the full freedom of that visitation, indeed she encouraged it as best she could. The Visitor himself said later that when he summoned sisters from other houses to speak to them, he was never denied for any reason nor did he know of any desire to distance sisters suspected of being opposed to the Mother. Indeed, he was free to move, visiting the various houses even without warning the Mother General in advance each time, and he was welcomed and courteously treated always and everywhere. Indeed, the sisters and superiors, especially the provincials, showed full trust and transparency in relations with the mandatory of the Holy See;31 and if at first some religious found it embarrassing or difficult to confide in him, this should be ascribed to her natural timidity rather than to repressive methods or prior suggestions. It is right to note all this here because it demonstrates the sincerity of the Mother’s submission to the Holy See and removes any shadow which might have fallen upon her.

As for the principal cause of the complaints, that is, the houses’ contributions to the Generalate, it was clear that the Mother had nothing to do with it and that it was a question of a lack of balance or common-sense in one superior or another. Perhaps the Mother had not been informed in the most minute detail of all that was happening around her, but certainly the money was destined for the purpose of maintaining the Institute. “Of this I am certain”, the Visitor attests, “it was not a matter of speculation nor the enrichment of her relatives”. On this thorny topic he also said: “I think I heard it said that Mother Gattorno, on discovering that the sisters were suffering in some house because of excessive stringency, complained to their respective superiors and protested, demanding that they be properly treated. But other sisters were responsible for making further invitations to send extraordinary gifts. This is how I see it. However I don’t believe that Mother Gattorno was ever two-faced; indeed, I am sure of it”.32

Countless proofs seem in fact to attest that the Mother not only took on her shoulders the serious burden of fund-collecting for the works of the Institute and contracted debts to provide for the houses, but in her correspondence with the superiors she urged them to take great care of the sisters entrusted to them. She wrote trenchantly to one provincial who was hesitant about giving help to certain houses in need: “You say you are ready to help those houses, but are afraid. Oh, what are you saying! I have often written to you to take care to help them all, and you must help them all!33 She also finally gave orders for the closure of a house, although it was so dear to her, that is, Santa Croce in Bolivia, because she had been told that the sisters were finding it too hard to keep going.34

As regards the administrative sector, one episode occurred which shows another dimension of Mother Rosa’s extraordinary virtue. Looking at the annual accounts, the Visitor realized that the balance was closed every year with a deficit, but that it was not carried over to the following year. In adding all these deficits, the total came to about 90,000 lire. Proceeding at this pace and accumulating those gaps every year, the Institute would shortly have found itself in difficulty. When the Mother was questioned on this, she said that every deficit had been balanced, and therefore it was not carried over to the following years. The Visitor replied that there must be another accounts book presenting the truth of the financial position; but the Mother answered that there was no other book, that that was the only one but that it was nonetheless true that the deficit had been covered. When the Visitor asked her how, she answered that it was a secret which she would never reveal to anyone.

She stuck to her answer, despite the prelate’s insistence and his observation that it was her duty to obey, given his office as envoy of the Holy See, and he even made a few threats. The Mother knew well that obedience in that matter pertained to the presentation of the accounts but not to the revelation of the spiritual events or miracles which God had been pleased to grant her. She had spoken of this to the priest who had long been her spiritual director, but humility forbade her telling others about the mysterious origin of the funds with which she settled the yearly deficits; she was ready to suffer serious trouble rather than unveil that sacred mystery.35

Another reason for the Apostolic Visitation was the Mother’s system of government. There were some weak points, not due to dishonesty but to the impelling needs resulting from events. Of course, it would have been excellent to form the religious in different groups according to the main specifications of their offices; Mother Rosa, as has been said, also keenly wanted worthy priests thoroughly dedicated to spiritual assistance in the houses and, in particular, she wanted in the novitiates excellent mistresses for the formation of the novices’ spirit. All this was occasionally lacking, at times because of gaps created by extrinsic circumstances over and above all good will, and they could not always be entirely remedied. The Constitutions of the Daughters of St. Anne, already definitively approved by the Holy See, did not distinguish different categories of religious according to the various fields of service. Only the missionaries received special preparation, in Rome and Piacenza. Later, in 1923, the “International College of the Missions” would be founded for this specific purpose.

Outcome of the Apostolic Visitation and recognition of the Mother’s uprightness ~ The Visitor nevertheless paid the Mother General a fine tribute: “Asked whether Mother Gattorno was upright in choosing the superiors of the large houses in Rome and Piacenza, I must answer that I never met superiors who did not deserve to be in that post. Mistakes can of course happen; but I could not say that [the Mother] allowed herself to be guided by secondary aims”36.

The purely external contacts the Visitor could have with the Mother certainly could not reveal to him the interior greatness of that soul or the solid temper of virtue in which, through the abundance of God’s gifts, she had been forged. Important, however, is the judgment he formed of her in the two years in which he was able to know her closely, together with the work she had founded: “I esteem the Servant of God as a woman of piety, of no ordinary mind and of great energy”37.

When such great gifts are placed unreservedly at the service of God and of the Church, they flourish and undoubtedly lead to holiness.

We believe in Rosa Gattorno’s total dedication to the Church not because of her frequent words of veneration and filial love for the Pope, nor because of the delicate attentions she showed on various anniversaries, but because of the exhausting works she accomplished to extend the Kingdom of God and because of her spirit, always attentive and most obedient to the slightest wish of the Church and of the Supreme Pontiff, eager as she was to walk safely with Christ and to act with him. She felt deeply that there is no fruitfulness in good where there is not full adherence to the faith and to the truth.

(1858-1900) Mystical experience told in the “Memorie” — The four types of infused prayer — Jealous custody of an ineffable secret — Heroism in the exercise of virtues — Mystical gifts and mysterious participation in the Passion of Christ: extraordinary experience of Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini — Passive purification and the rare “caresses” of her Good.

Mystical experience told in the “Memorie” ~ When the alabaster jar had been broken and the last drops of ointment poured onto Christ’s head, the whole house in Bethany was filled with the sweet fragrance of the precious essence; but far more precious gifts filled the soul of Mary, Lazarus’ sister. From that moment, her mind, heart and spirit knew no other measure than Christ’s infinite love. All Christendom recognizes in Mary of Bethany the one whom Jesus himself favored, showing his fondness for her openly.

Mother Rosa also knew the secret way to Jesus’ heart, she had felt its mysterious impulses since her early widowhood. We know how generously she then broke the alabaster jar of her body with the harshest austerities and poured out all her soul in the One she called her Good; the life which is recounted here is a truly perfect immolation for the glory and pleasure of the Father. For this reason, so generous a soul did not lack the privilege of unitive love, a genuine mystical experience which became a radical process of inner transformation.

This is evident above all in her Memorie, those simple and unadorned accounts of her inner life written at the explicit desire of her Good. Indeed, she says: “So I remained for many days and months without writing and he gave me a chastisement I deserved, but it was so gentle and sweet that I could only answer him: forgive me, my Good” (M. 1.1, p. 155).

We say further that these pages will disappoint eyes avid for mysterious revelations or accustomed to the elegant literary style with which other privileged persons dress up the accounts of their spiritual experiences. These writings all have the humility of a recorded account, they are uncluttered and their style is almost crude. In spite of this, they fully reveal Mother Rosa’s soul: one can glimpse her exquisite sensitivity, her tenacious will, ever striving for the conquests of the kingdom, her generous spirit of sacrifice, her purest love of Christ and immense faith in him.

She speaks of herself calmly, as if narrating to herself what she was living in her inmost depths. The episodes that concern her are only mentioned because they caused deep spiritual reverberations within her. Her extraordinary mystical experience is presented in the Memorie as her only school, extended through the years, which constantly provided her spirit with a great store of knowledge and interior experiences.

Her mind, less and less a prisoner of the circumstances, continued to open out to new understanding, to immense possibilities which broadened her horizons and nourished her imagination, intuition and creativity.

Anyone who is dominated by the Spirit really becomes a “new creature”, acquires unsuspected potential, dimensions unknown to human life.

Although there is no hint in the Memorie that they are addressed to any specific person, they are a fundamental document and possess the riches and value of a clear, irreplaceable testimony which continues to be amazingly up to date.

The four types of infused prayer ~ These pages are actually an inexhaustible mine of precious gems, because they disclose to us the wonderful work wrought by God in that great soul.

First of all, we see in them the loftiest infused prayer, marked by the most reliable and fruitful characteristics of surprising apostolic energy. Theologians specialized in mysticism establish four characteristics proper to this level of orison or contemplation, that is passivity, the experience of God’s presence, the special enjoyment or fruition of it, the impulse to the generous acts of the soundest virtues. Now it seems to us that all these properties are effortlessly found in Rosa Gattorno’s prayer.

As to passivity, it is seen in almost every page of her Memorie; that type of prayer, or rather contemplation, was wholly a gift of divine liberality, independent of any effort or commitment of the Mother, so inevitable was the rapture of the subject and her close emotional union; indeed it sometimes immediately followed deep sorrows and diabolical suggestions, while she was in a state of complete abandonment, silent before the tabernacle.

On other occasions, when some external task was pressing, she had to fight against the intense attraction of that lofty intimacy with God.

But the opposite also occurred: when she would have liked to be immersed in those sweet digressions or at least to prolong them, the union would cease instantly, and her soul would be left arid and even subject to temptation.

However, her humility often elicited fear of those extraordinary gifts so that far from seeking them, she was filled with wonder that the most High would bend down to her and, as it were, warded him off: “My God, what suffering is mine! and the more misshapen I see myself, the closer my God comes to me. Ah, do not fill me with horror, have pity on me! My Good, what horror!” (M. 4.1, p. 15).

Jealous custody of an ineffable secret ~ From these words it is clear that Mother Rosa neither encouraged her imagination towards those heights, nor deceived herself about her experiences; she felt she was the humblest slave of the Lord’s work, to which she submitted in perfect docility. Indeed, she had great fear that something might show: “I am like someone who is keeping something hidden and is constantly afraid that the moment will come when they will see it…” (M. 4.1, p. 19; 4.1, p. 66; 4.1 pp. 71-72 and pp. 76-77; 4.2. pp. 2-3).

Because of this fear, she would have liked to hide any of the consequences of her long prayer vigils and most intense participation in Christ’s Passion, of which we will speak later; her pallor and the visible exhaustion of her body suggested a physical ailment, so she accepted the remedies offered to her by her secretaries who then made no further investigations. For the same reason she was adamant about not wanting anyone to enter her cell in Piacenza, a refuge of great austerity and the Tabor of her spirit, for fear that a hint of the favors God lavished upon her might be betrayed.

This jealous privacy reached the point of inducing her to make a long journey to fetch a forgotten object rather than permit a religious to enter that room. Once, in fact, when some missionaries were leaving for America, the Mother had prepared the tickets and money for the journey; having made her usual exhortations to the departing sisters and given them her last embrace, she set out for Rome, forgetting those indispensable items on her table. She had to telegraph Rome; as soon as she had arrived there and realized what she had forgotten, she immediately set out on the return journey to Piacenza, not admitting that there might be any other way of resolving the inconvenience.1

All this clearly shows how far Mother Rosa was from being gratified by extraordinary experiences, even of a spiritual kind, and how well she could guard the secret of her Good who deigned every now and then to elevate her to such heights.

She then felt the unspeakable effects of his presence: tranquillity, sweetness, and peace flooded her heart, making her feel the closeness of the divine, of the ineffable; the darkness and doubts of her conscience and the oppressive anxieties of governing vanished. It seemed to her that she was led by the hand in the grandiose work of the Institute and had boundless strength within her. The gift of wisdom, present to an extraordinary degree in that most faithful soul, disposed her to receiving special inspirations and lights of the Spirit who had enriched her intellectual capacities; and she penetrated the mystery with immense delight and the sweetest wonder. In that luminous and inebriating ocean she felt her natural smallness more acutely than ever and profoundly humiliated herself, confessing that all she was then enjoying came from God. The intimate testimony of her conscience felt safe in that brightness, as though God were speaking to her and approving her way of working, blessing her sacrifices, penances and the dedication with which she sought to honor him. At times she was perplexed about the authenticity of that most unique process, not knowing whether one practice or another dictated by her fervent imagination were truly pleasing to God; but in those moments of union she felt the response of her Beloved with ineffable delight. On some rare occasions, she was also illumined as to future events and then her complete abandonment in God’s arms had the intensity of the holocaust of love. These were the rarest effects of the grace of union in that privileged soul, as emerges from her writings.

Because of this wonderful familiarity with her Good, Rosa Gattorno could well say with the Bride of the Song of Songs: “I am my Beloved’s and my Beloved is mine” (Sg 6:3).

But what bliss she drew from it is not easy to imagine, nor did she succeed in describing it.

In her various attempts at telling her director about it, we see that her efforts were often in vain; her means of expression were totally inadequate and one only catches glimpses of the divine brightness which invaded her.

In these writings,2 she says again and again that she is incapable of describing or expressing her sentiments, experiences and emotions in words; there is only her wonder at the gift she has received.

This is also a phenomenon that theologians specialized in mysticism observe in saints, since their sublime experiences exceed all earthly language; and once the light shines no more, the mind no longer reflects it, thoughts return to their usual, ordinary state, and the soul no longer feels permeated by the divine: all that remains is a heartrending nostalgia.

But every now and then, the sisters close to her saw in their Mother something particularly fascinating and almost luminous which delightfully entranced them; this happened especially when she had stayed longer in the solitude of her Spartan cell: Some risked a question: “Mother, who knows what the Lord gave you?”. But, amiably, she would immediately change the subject.

Those who were in charge of her laundry, noticed that the Mother gave it to them already more or less washed, obviously to hide the traces of the wound in her side; but her precaution did not always fully succeed, since the attentive eyes of her sisters several times found signs of her mysterious suffering. In fact, we know from the pages of the Memorie how, while she was praying, she would feel her chest burning and her ribs lifting; she felt faint from the force of the effect. Then the old scar, made by the crucifix she had worn for many years bound to her chest and embedded in the flesh, would open and bleed.

On other occasions, for some relief she would have to fetch cloths soaked in ice-cold water to try to calm the burning sensation which those sublime, sweetest transports gave her.

Heroism in the exercise of virtues ~ However, the most reliable sign of the divine origin of the events told so far about Mother Rosa’s mystical experience was the very sound impetus which she derived from the exercise of all the virtues. The multiple and exhausting activity of governing the Institute required a commitment that was certainly out of the ordinary and a spirit of tolerance often heroic, so numerous were the hostilities and contradictions which beset her outside it. The worry of providing for the many temporal needs, the necessary forbearance to put up with the defects and defections, the motherly assistance she owed the religious near and far. Mother Rosa drew light and strength for all this from her lofty union with God.

“What sweetness you have brought to my spirit! You have filled me with it, and I rejoice among so many tribulations. Everything for the Work of my God! I would have had myself broken into pieces [so strong] was my desire to spend myself in it and for it!” (M. 4.1, p. 58).

God’s Work was a very frequent subject in these conversations with her Beloved and it also gave rise to wistful longing when, like Mary Magdalene, she was forced to tear herself away from the Master’s feet, to concentrate on her many external tasks. In the Mother, the existence of her enormously busy activity of government and, at the same time, so exalted and frequent an experience of intimate union with her Good is astounding.

As well as spiritual ardor, an ever more radical abandonment of earthly things and all that was purely human was growing in that most generous heart.

“For a long time”, she wrote in 1872, “everything earthly and human has been having a certain curious effect on me […]. When I see certain things become beautiful and fall into place for the future and have to do something to preserve them […], O, foolish woman that you are [I say] you tire yourself out and tomorrow you no longer have anything! This is continuous and in everything; but it does not prevent me from working and thinking about consolidating God’s Work, and this has another effect on me; it seems to me that I am working for something that has no end, and that it is of God and for God, so that for him all seems to me to be eternal. But if I then have to think specifically of the sisters to obtain more things for them, my thoughts are immediately warped, and everything seems pointless to me. This is how it is for me: what a feeling I have when I realize that they are thinking of getting me a new pair of shoes! I immediately say: My God, if I am not certain of wearing this pair out, how can I accept the new pair? And only to think that they will give them to me grieves me; I must reprimand the person who had them made for me and immediately give them away […]. Oh, if my Daughters only felt what I feel, not only would they not bother me with telling me what I need, but they would let me go around with half my clothes and patched slippers.! My God, I always pray for it: make them feel a little of what this poor most unworthy servant of yours feels!” (M. 4.1, pp. 111-114).

Even more generous was her readiness to sacrifice her children, rather than let them fall into sin: “I must confess that the good and the love I feel for these two children is enormous: yet I willingly submit to the mortal wound of their death, rather than to see them wicked and offenders of God, my one All” (M. 4, p. 120).

However, the principal teaching of the divine Teacher which Rosa had learned by heart was humility, indeed, the loving quest for lowliness. So when the Mother saw God’s work and human interest in her increasing, her self-esteem diminished and she found no words to express her nothingness. She recognized she had trotted like God’s little donkey wherever he had sent her: “Sweetest command”, she adds, “that inebriates and fortifies, makes every task gentle and sweet and most enjoyable”; but she always trembled in that divine service for fear of ruining God’s plan and of not reaching its fulfilment. This sentiment was dictated by her conviction of her ignorance, due, as she said, to her “wickednesses”, which is why she claimed she was so unintelligent as to be unable to understand properly the exquisiteness of God’s words.

The sincerity of these feelings is apparent in her inclination for humiliations, to the point of fearing that she might be deprived of them. One day, as she was praying for the conversion of a religious who caused her deep suffering with calumnies against her and God’s Work, she suddenly stopped short, troubled by the thought that if this person converted, she would no longer offend her: “If I don’t have that [problem] any longer, my God, I will not be able to have these humiliations and I shall be deprived of them: what will be left to me? […]. Oh, I find too much consolation in humiliations to be able to escape them!” (M. 4.2, pp. 70-71).

She was therefore deeply pained to see some of her sisters who were not walking on the path of humility, thereby depriving themselves of many graces and joys in the spiritual life. What would she not have done to enlighten them on this point!

Her concern for divine glory and for the contempt of earthly things, affections and honors was accompanied in that magnanimous heart by an ever living desire for immolation. Already wearing forms of mortification and instruments of penance, she thought she could not bear any more of them, but that love was asking her for yet more; after some hesitation, she decided to bind a new and heavy chain around her waist, which soon caused sores and made her disciplines even more cruel. She sometimes wondered whether she had exaggerated, especially as in those years she was living without a real spiritual director; but the sweetness of spirit which repaid her or even the unexpected healing of her wounded flesh and some inner voice which she seemed to hear in prayer ended by reassuring her; and the mortification of her body became a most acute need of her spirit. “I have never had such enjoyment”, she wrote, “as when I hung from the cross; and every time I climbed up it was an ascent that brought me to the sweet dwelling-place of my Good”. (M. 4.1, pp. 22-24).

By the tone of these words one can understand the nostalgia she must have felt for Piacenza when she was distant from it for the duties of her office. “Rome”, she exclaimed at the beginning of 1874, “you have become my exile, because in this house I can do none of my beloved penances! […]. If I think about my dear cell in Piacenza, I feel such an affliction […]. My Good, what suffering this is! But for you I put up with everything. The longing I feel to go to the Piacenza house soon is so great that there are moments when I commend myself to God, so as not to faint; I will escape by night! Finally I go there in my thoughts and why? To be able to satisfy myself by scourging until the blood comes, for which I have been thirsting unspeakably for days” (M. 4.2, p. 28; 4.1, p. 64; 4.1, p. 28). In Piacenza in fact, she had tasted the fervor and incomparable gifts of the first-fruits in religious life precisely with her extraordinary penances which she could only do in the remote solitude of her cell; but in Rome, in rented rooms or in the small houses,3 she would not have been able to abandon herself to this severity without the sisters noticing.

Mystical gifts and mysterious participation in the Passion of Christ: extraordinary experience of Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini ~ Thus the charisms of her unitive experience brought Mother Rosa not only the sweetness that is a prelude to heaven, but also the precious accompaniment of the sounder virtues which are becoming to the true Bride and make her worthy to follow the Lamb in the mystical nuptials. We believe that this is the best confirmation of the authenticity of her gifts. Mystical gifts are a purely gratuitous donation of divine goodness and are not really essential to define a person’s holiness; but they often accompany it and are given as a reward for rare impulses of generosity or as the means for a specific mission in God’s Church. They are certainly not found in the spiritual desert of souls that are dissipated or penetrated by evil, because they presuppose God’s love and are the most exalted manifestation of it. While in souls devoid of virtue there can at times be an unusual flash in communications with God, it is essential to proceed with great caution before believing in it, because it can easily involve the deception of the angel of darkness who likes to appear as an angel of light.

That is why Jesus Christ responds to these splendid follies of love with that liberality which is his own and in which he never lets himself be surpassed by his creatures.

As well as the charisms of infused prayer, the Savior gave his Servant a mysterious participation in the sufferings of his Passion. There are many references to this in the Memorie, but it is preferable to base them on the extrinsic testimonies of her sisters who witnessed them at different times and in different circumstances.

Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini tells us (and she also testified to it in the informative process in Rome) that on Holy Friday of 1886, in Italy and preparing to leave for America, she managed by great insistence and scheming to enter the Mother’s little room in Rome; here she was as usual spending the sacred days of the Passion in absolute withdrawal and fasting.

It was in the afternoon, when Jesus’ agony is commemorated. “Then finding myself beside the poor Mother”, Sr. Anna Camilla says, “I noticed such an expression on her beloved face that I cannot describe, although the image still endures as though recently observed. What kind of suffering did she feel? […]. I only say that, in the state in which I saw her, I supposed that her death must be close. I offered to help her, but she wanted absolutely nothing and begged me to leave her in peace […]. That day I also saw on my Mother’s broad forehead, clearly marked and distinct, the impression of the Redeemer’s crown of thorns. I did not see the thorns but the deep wounds they had made…”.

The truly touching account of the extraordinary experience which Sr. Anna Camilla exceptionally shared continues. She saw the spasms and signs of the Passion increase in the Mother’s tortured body, and was moved to deep pity, she tried to feel her pulse, gently raising her arm, stretched out as though she were on the Cross. “I saw no wound”, she tells, “in the beloved Mother’s hands, but I felt something in each palm like a hard nail formed of a growth of flesh. I realized it was a dislocation of her bones and the tendons with the muscles were contorting almost as though to crush the bones, piercing her hands and my heart”.

However, Sr. Anna Camilla did not only feel disturbed and compassionate; from the Mother’s painful limbs a mysterious pain was also transfused in her.

“I confess”, she says, “that the spasms she communicated to me were so violent in my hands and arms that I could no longer stand, and would have certainly fainted if the good Mother, realizing this, had not said to me: “Now, enough; sit down close to me and rest”.

“For how long”, the sister asked her, “have these things been happening to you?”. “Twentyeight years”, the Mother replied; hence from 1858, that is, from the time of her widowhood, or she could have meant that this had first happened to her at the age of twenty-eight, during the first years of her widowhood, in any case.

In short, she told her that every Friday she had similar sufferings, which were shared by anyone who touched her, especially on Good Friday. She imposed absolute secrecy on Sr. Anna Camilla about what she had discovered on that occasion, and the sister kept Mother Rosa’s secret until after her death.4

That this was what happened can also be deduced from a similar experience which involved Sr. Anna Cunegonda Pacini.

“One day”, she tells, “it was a Friday, and when I came across the Servant of God, as usual I came close to her to kiss her hand, and felt a sensation as though I had burned my lips. I asked the Servant of God if she felt at all feverish and she smiled. I kissed the same hand again, and when I said that I felt my lips burning, the Servant of God said: so you will pronounce the Most Holy Name of Jesus more sweetly. I noted on her hand something like the mark of a bruise […]. I also point out that on that day it was exceptional that I had been able to meet the Servant of God, because on Fridays we only saw her in church; she did not even come to the refectory”.5

Mother Rosa’s great fear was that this and other events would be leaked to those who were close to her; and she was so tormented by the idea that she said nothing about them for a long time, not even to the person acting as her spiritual director during the first years of the Institute, because she did not trust in his discretion.6

Enveloped like this in silence, she was often beset by great doubts, fearing on the one hand that she was deceived by the evil spirit, while on the other, it really seemed to her that she had unmistakable proof of the divine work within her: “Living without [spiritual] direction is a cruel torture”, she wrote; and she was all the more perplexed when those near her insisted that she take care of herself, since in conscience she should make sure that she had the strength needed to govern the Institute, which depended entirely upon her. However, she was unable to adapt to a renunciation of the austerities from which she drew such union with God; on the other hand, events proved that she was always ready for the work and duties of her office, although her health was precarious.

Passive purifications and the rare “caresses” of her Good ~ Then she had various temptations which disturbed her like a storm of darkness and increased her doubt that she might be at the mercy of the forces of evil. But when the light returned, she felt sure she was walking on the right road and found the courage to continue (M. 3, pp. 19-20).

“Now that I am writing, because I find myself so peaceful, I would say that it would be impossible for any kind of temptation to make me doubt… [But], since it is the divine will that this happen, it would not surprise me if, in a few hours, I were to find myself on a rough sea and not to know how to save myself…” (M. 4.2, pp. 7-8).

This state of things lasted for about fifteen years. In the meantime she faithfully wrote down whatever happened inside her soul; one day, she was to find the right priest worthy of her complete trust, to give him those pages and hear his opinion. That priest was Fr. Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte from Naples, later Cardinal and for years Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne.

Leafing through those accounts for her director, we come to know the inmost drama of Mother Rosa, since the richness of her sweetest gifts of infused prayer were accompanied, as usual, by those painful tests which theologians call passive purifications since they all depend on God and are totally unmotivated by the soul. Previously, in Chapter V, we mentioned them; here, rather than the infirmities of the body and the persecutions of men, the arid sorrows of the spirit and the harassment of the devil should be considered.

Her spiritual aridity reached such a level that the Mother often thought she was on the brink of perdition: “Ah, how sorrowful is my present state! My poor soul is alone, isolated in the midst of the great world, orphaned […]. A turbulent whisper now dominates it among the desperation of the damned; My poor soul, in the despair of the damned, finds it has lost its very Being. I cannot find him anywhere. Yes my God! I go to your tabernacle and find myself as though dumbstruck. Wherever I look I see only a precipice; I look at my deeds, to see if I can find any comfort in them […]. However hard I look, I find I am completely deprived […]; everything is dispelled at the appearance of my nothingness. What sufferings! I do not speak of the fear that causes this state in me: I can only say these are the fires of hell. I have lost my Beloved, the only object of my existence!” (M 3, p. 27-28).

The temptation of desperation was sometimes so violent that she was terrified. “On all sides there are excruciating troubles and all ways are barred to me; I see only a great precipice that drags me towards it: it is despair. And the force with which it draws me is such that, were it not for the divine power that upholds me, I could not resist without falling into it […]. Then, without thinking of anything, I abandon myself on the pillow of faith, unable to see who upholds me and the Being of my life. I know nothing, I see nothing, I do not know where he is or what he is doing […]. You alone can give me life”.

But in that darkness, besides holding firm to the faith, she gave herself more generously to prayer and penance. She would have liked to cast herself on the ground and be undone before the Almighty. “The long vigils of the night tear my soul apart; once they were a comfort to me… [The night] was sweet rest for me, while I spent most of it on my knees; now, prostrate on the ground with my arms stretched out on the floor in the form of a cross […], I feel I can bear it no longer; when I get up I find myself shattered and utterly empty of any good feeling” (M. 3, p. 29). It even seemed to her that her communions were unworthy: “I am abandoned by God and my communions are sacrileges! So I gloomily thought, withdrawn in my room” (M. 4.2, pp. 2, 4).

Under the weight of such anguish, the toils of government and the thousand temporal cares of providing for the houses of the Institute seemed nothing to her; indeed, she found relief in these and similar external tribulations.

“Tribulations alone are a comfort to me; the gloomy thought which, like a dismal voice, tells me: you are damned! […] weighs so heavily on my soul that I am in agony” (M. 1.2, p. 96).

It is not surprising that the devil made his rage felt with violent harassment against a soul so tried and yet so rooted in the love of God; the Mother says, in fact, that sometimes her bed was shaken until she fell out of it, that she had several repugnant apparitions and that at times she was molested by the evil one even by day. But she cared little for such sufferings, knowing where they came from; what weighed on her heavily, instead, were the terrible shadows of conscience of which we have spoken above.

God was purifying her with fatherly providence and preparing her for the highest degrees of charity. In those desolations, in fact, she felt her own nothingness and the vanity of every good apart from the Absolute; sustained by grace, she rose to him with all her will, seeking nothing outside him. To his handmaid, who sought him in those desolate agonies and in the holy folly of the Cross, God would then suddenly show himself with ineffable tenderness, and also favor her with generous and unexpected help for the needs of the Institute.

Such marks of the heavenly Father’s kindness must have greatly encouraged Mother Rosa on her hard journey; they were signs of approval of her work and of the way she was walking.

What we have tried to say in these pages seems to us to show the special indwelling of the Holy Spirit in this singular soul, so that, amid the troubled events of so long a life, in the continual alternation of light and shadow, of darkness and luminous, promising dawns, it can be said that this life was consumed as a most pure holocaust for the sole glory of God, to whom Mother Rosa dedicated every moment she lived in a most intense striving for union.
