(1858-1900) A miraculous event — Steadfast faith lived in the foundation and governance of the Institute — Faith to the point of martyrdom and missionary impetus — Meetings with charismatic people and future founders — Rapture in contemplation of the mysteries of the Incarnation and the Redemption — Faith put to the test and miraculous cures.

A miraculous event ~ One event is linked to the origins of Rosa Gattorno’s vocation which has something of the miraculous about it and deserves mention as it impressed a distinctive character upon her spirituality.

While living as a widow in her parent’s house, she used to spend long hours at night praying before a large crucifix, pondering the anguish and sorrow of her soul, especially after she had received the pressing invitation to consecrate herself totally to God and to give life to a new religious institute. Once, feeling deeper anguish than usual, she turned to Christ crucified saying to him: “But you see, Lord, that I must also think of the children you have given me!”. Suddenly, while she was praying, the figure of the crucified Christ came unstuck from the Cross and fell into her arms. At first believing that this had happened by accident, she fixed the figure back on the Cross, and continued praying. But it came unstuck again and fell.

Mother Rosa continued her prayers without giving it another thought and a little later went to bed.

The next day she told faithful Manin, the servant, that she had not managed to fix the image of Christ to the Cross firmly; the good woman offered to do it for her thinking she would be more successful, as in fact Rosa Gattorno requested.

However, when night came and she was praying in front of it as usual, the crucified Christ figure again fell into her arms. So the next day, she arranged with Manin to have a carpenter fix the sacred image to the cross more firmly, because she did not want to be further disturbed while praying. But that night when the Mother had started her prayers, again the Christ figure became unstuck and, as previously, fell into her arms.1

She then understood God’s sign and was deeply moved; it meant that she was to be completely united with the crucified Jesus and to undertake his mission, whatever the cost, sacrificing herself like her Savior for the good of souls. “So you want me to carry the Cross”, she said lovingly and submissively to Jesus: and from that time she never nailed the image back on the cross; it became very dear to her and she kept it with her, jealously guarded in her cell in Piacenza.2

Steadfast faith lived in the foundation and governance of the Institute ~ After that night marked with a miracle, faith, already so resplendent in Rosa Gattorno, shone with a new light in her soul. It made her measure great and small things against the Blood and Wounds of the Man God; as this light brought her into the depths of the mystery, it also showed her the paths of her new apostolic undertaking, impressing upon her wonderful impulses of the most exalted love for her religious and for all those for whom her tireless work was intended.

The Mother’s way of unfailingly ending her letters by saying: “I embrace you in my crucified Christ” became proverbial among the Daughters of St. Anne. In giving a piece of advice she would end by saying: “There, run to your crucified Christ, and if you have faith, you will certainly obtain what you ask”; then as a last resort or a pledge of certainty, she would still keep to her crucified Christ: “Oh, my crucified One”, she would say, “will see to everything. My crucified One will safeguard his Work. My crucified One will come to the help of his servant”.

She spoke of him so passionately that she roused emotion; during her conferences to the community, she would always introduce this topic into everything, so that she truly walked and made others walk in the light that shines from the Cross of Christ, a sign and place of fidelity. When a soul is penetrated by faith, what Jesus said happens, that is, the whole of life is guided by truth and shines with God’s justice: “The lamp of your body is your eye. When your eye is sound, your whole body too is filled with light; but when it is diseased your body too will be all darkness. See to it then that the light inside you is not darkness. If, therefore, your whole body is filled with light, and no trace of darkness, it will be light entirely, as when the lamp shines on you with its rays” (Lk 11:34).

In this regard, Mother Gattorno confessed that God had given her the gift of a profound and unshakeable faith: “Faith”, she said, “was given to me by God, who studded it with diamonds”.3

She not only meant that her conviction of all that is taught by the Catholic Church was indestructible, but that she held it in the highest esteem, drew from it enthusiasm for her work and nothing in the world could take that treasure from her. Since the early years of her youth her heart had been so steeped in Christ’s words that she transmitted to the soul of others the overwhelming joy of believing and following the teachings of the Master, as when she taught the Christian doctrine to the people at San Francesco d’Albaro and when, more grown-up, she was a very active leader of the associations in the Diocese of Genoa. But the full splendor of her faith appeared when she was preparing to found the Institute; she was brought to do so only by the love of Christ, she had no fear of her own weakness or of the scarcity of means; so, as we have amply told in these pages, she overcame disconcerting obstacles and defections. Even a priest tried to dissuade her from the work she had begun and presented himself one day in Piacenza saying: “But what are you doing here? Close down and send everyone home, which would be better”. But the generous woman replied with simplicity that she feared no obstacles: that it was a work of God and therefore had to continue; she was certain and it had been confirmed to her by the Pope, for Pius IX had indeed told her that the work would certainly last until the end of the world.4

In the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, next to the humble apostolate of charitable assistance to the sick and the instruction of the young, almost straight away Mother Rosa also felt the missionary ideal, in all its grandiose fullness. “When the sisters left for the missions”, one witness said, “you just had to hear her discourses, so enflamed with faith!”. “You must go down there to save lots and lots of souls for me and send them to heaven”, she said to Sr. Anna Gerarda Canovi, when she had chosen her for Africa; “You are going to foreign lands”, she said to those who were leaving for Bolivia in South America, “without knowing what you will come across. You might meet people who will attack our religion, but there is only one true religion and that is ours. Don’t let it ever happen that instead of converting others you let yourselves be perverted! Be strong, never stray from the crucified Christ, I give him to you as a pledge…. If you find yourselves caught up in some revolution”, she added, “and you are tempted in your faith, give up even your life!”.5

Thus she presumed that the missionaries had an inclination for martyrdom; for her part, martyrdom was very close, indeed she desired it: “Oh, if only I were granted to shed my blood for the faith!”, she was frequently heard to exclaim. “How I would like to die a martyr, to purge my sins and see Jesus soon!”.6

With her discourses she roused them to such a pitch of enthusiasm for martyrdom that according to the testimonies of some sisters, she left them disappointed that it had not happened to them.

More than in her words however, the indestructible faith of Mother Rosa was expressed in her deeds. In that difficult and troubled historical period, dominated by anticlericalism and ruthless attacks on the Church, it was very easy for the press to spread criticism of the Pope and in the political conflicts, for people to speak ill of religion. In varying degrees, the press also influenced the conversations of believers: but if someone permitted himself in the Mother’s presence to echo the press and to make some pejorative remark about the Supreme Pontiff, she immediately interrupted, no matter who was speaking, declaring that she did not want to hear anything because, since the Pope was concerned, he had to be spoken of well in all regards, nor would she tolerate any kind of criticism.7

These stances taken in defense of the Pope and religion were accompanied by her efforts to spread the right doctrine. “I would like to convert everyone to our faith”, she would say in fiery tones; and she would insist that the superiors and teachers do their utmost to imbue the hearts of the children with the truth of religion in the best way possible. Nor did she worry about expenses; for the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary, so flourishing in her time, she had rented premises adjacent to the Generalate in Rome; she was generous with presents to induce those young girls to come there, and she would often go and have friendly talks with them. She also wanted a room for the Luigini next to the Church, in order to instruct those little ones and prepare them for their First Communion.

She offered the sisters all the means she had available for their instruction in the Christian doctrine; she herself continued to give catechism classes to the young professed until the last years of her life. For the novices and postulants, she arranged for two sisters to give them a lesson in religion every day: twice a month they all had to attend the lesson given by an ecclesiastic.

Her energy and zeal in speaking was such when she was talking about religion that the sisters competed for seats in the front row. In the Chapter of 1888, which was chaired by Cardinal Alimonda, it once happened that the preacher of the spiritual retreat saw almost all the religious leaving towards the end of his preaching, and so he asked the few that remained whether some misfortune had occurred; but they had left to hasten to the room where immediately afterwards the Mother was to give a talk. Having been told of the incident, Mother Rosa obviously gave them a serious reprimand. Nevertheless, this event illustrates the sisters’ delight in their Mother’s instruction. It was also noticed that when she spoke to the novices about God’s commandments and the directives of the Church, she would refer to particular cases and give practical examples, but with such communicative love that she instilled in those souls the highest esteem for the Lord’s laws.8

However, Mother Gattorno’s faith shone out in her life even more than in her words: for her, transparency of life was essential to faith. “Remember,” she would say to the superiors, “that we are like the Crucifix above the altar, on view to all the faithful, and therefore we should not let the sisters see any fault in us. The superior is like a candelabra that must give light to everyone”.9 For her part, she displayed such closeness and communion with God as to deeply involve anyone who spoke to her; the talks she gave were always exalted and never frivolous or superficial.

When she was invited to send some of her religious to the kindergarten and school in Caccivio, she went to see whether she could place the sisters there. When she entered the classroom, all the little girls knelt. They refused to stand up, even when the Mother suggested that they rise, before she had blessed them. She satisfied them, said a few wise words to the school-mistresses, then addressing the children, urged them to treasure the teaching imparted to them. They listened to her with bated breath, almost bewitched by her presence; finally they asked to be blessed again: “Yes, yes,” the Mother answered, “may the Lord bless you and make you all good”. Thus the memory of the Mother never faded from those little hearts; on the contrary, it happened later that the school-mistress and some of her pupils became religious among the Daughters of St. Anne; one of them, Sr. Anna Pasqualina, tells the story; she was superior in Salsomaggiore in 1916.10

Those who came to visit the Mother General had a similar impression that she was in contact with the divine; her secretaries, as they accompanied the visitors to the door, would hear comments full of admiration, such as: “That woman is up there rather than down here”.

Many other Daughters of St. Anne admitted that their decision to consecrate themselves to God was due to the conversations they had had with Mother Gattorno and indeed wrote to her: “After my talk with you I can no longer resist; I feel that the Lord wants me in your Institute”. Everyone can plainly see the depth of the beneficial influence which such a Mother exercised on her religious, and especially on those who had the fortune to be constantly beside her. They are unanimous in recalling her slightest words because they were always in tune with the supernatural, the sweet impulses she drew from her love of heavenly things and, more specifically, her training in how to converse with God, overcome temptations and distractions, draw fruit from the sacraments and maintain the proper respect for the great gift of their vocation.

Therefore Mother Rosa really was the lighted lamp placed on the stand to illuminate everyone in her house.

Faith to the point of martyrdom and missionary impetus ~ However, she also liked to be with those who were closest to God and therefore more penetrated and transformed by the faith. In her travels, knowing that in one city or other there were persons renowned for their special virtues, she never failed to visit them and talk to them informally. She had done this since she was a young girl with the humble Capuchin brother who today is venerated on the altars, St. Francis of Camporosso, because he spoke with inspiration of God’s affairs and cheered and encouraged her in her tribulations: indeed it is said that this holy religious predicted all her travail as Foundress, since once, putting his hand on her head, he exclaimed: “Poor Rosa, what I see, what I see! What you will have to go through! Oh how many sisters, how many sisters I see who are to follow you!”.11

In Naples she met another lay Franciscan, Fra Angelo, who had a deep love for the Child Jesus and with whom she often conversed; as she did with Fr. Menna, Rector of the Church of St. Anne, well known for his great virtue and who had received many of the Lord’s gifts. At Santa Maria Capua Vetere she used to like to talk to Fr. Donato Giannotti to whom she went for confession: he founded an institute which was then entrusted to the Grey Friars of Fr. Ludovico da Casoria.12

Figures distinguished for their heroic virtues such as the future blesseds, Fr. Annibale di Francia and Fr. Giacomo Cusmano, also often turned to her in their search for sisters for their charitable works; however, having recognized the differences in their charisms, she subsequently established new foundations herself.13

Through her inner liveliness and habitual enlightenment of faith, Rosa Gattorno admirably combined the qualities of both active and contemplative life. Her natural temperament, in itself very excitable and sensitive to pain, found a reliable support in her intuitions, so that she enjoyed great peace and amazing self-control even in the most unforeseen circumstances; it led her to prompt and clear discernment of many of the things to be done for the Institute, and prodigious, tireless activity. Since she constantly remained in the presence of her Good and in perfect communion with him, from him she derived all her human and spiritual faculties and received the clearest directives in the complex governance of her Institute and the unfailing contribution of his omnipotence.

Meetings with charismatic people and future founders ~ Aware that she possessed an immeasurable treasure and of the great need to trust in God in all circumstances, Mother Gattorno wanted the spirit of faith and trusting abandonment in the arms of the Father to flourish in the Daughters of St. Anne to a supreme degree. Hence the many pious practices she prescribed, to revive their memory of the various mysteries of religion and to give them an experience of them. These practices were differently distributed in the course of the year according to the liturgical cycle; thus she wanted the month of January to be dedicated to the Eternal Father14 with daily prayers, for which she obtained indulgences from Leo XIII; she wanted March, May, June and October to be celebrated, in accordance with the Church’s tradition, in honor of St. Joseph, Mary Most Holy and the Sacred Heart; the month of July was obviously solemn because of the Feast of St. Anne, with abstinence every Wednesday and a day of fasting on the eve of the feast. She also wanted certain events prepared and celebrated with special solemnity.

However, she was not content with making her sisters live and enjoy the splendors of our faith through worship; she also strove to communicate them to the people as best she could. For this purpose she wanted the lovely Church in Rome built next to the Generalate and from the first year that it was open for worship, she wanted the month of May to be celebrated solemnly and with a great display, without bothering about the expense, although the Institute was extremely poor and burdened by many debts. In those early times the Via Merulana was not densely populated; it was in the heart of the city’s poorest neighborhoods and preachers were sometimes slightly uncomfortable there; but this never dismayed the Mother, and in the end the fruits were abundant. The hymns she had the religious sing were a great help in persuading large numbers of people to go there and to stay willingly. She drew much enjoyment from this, especially when she heard that this singing had led to conversions. Indeed, the singing of a sister with a beautiful voice was once applauded in church; the Mother did not like this at all, and summoning the sister said to her “What should we do? […]. It means I shall not have you sing any more”.

Indeed, she no longer allowed her to sing solo parts.15

With regard to her devotion to Mary most holy, something truly unique in addition to what we have already recounted should be mentioned here: the long 40-day fast for the Madonna della Guardia of Genoa. Dumbfounded by the abundance of graces God was giving her and eager to respond to him ever better, while she was still in the world she had rented a small room and spent 40 days there absorbed in meditation, fasting on bread and water; she spent the whole day there in prayer and many hours in the sanctuary. Such was the abundance of divine favors that filled her in this holy place that she habitually called that period her “days of paradise”. Once, in Genoa, talking to Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, she mentioned the Monte della Guardia and exclaimed: “Oh, how lovely it was up there in that solitude!”.16

During her journeys in Italy she often took the opportunity to make long visits to the most important Marian shrines; but the sisters who accompanied her could never keep up with her long and exalted contemplation, which went beyond all the limits of human endurance. Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza and Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega went with her to Loreto four times: prostrate on the bare paving stones, the Mother would remain absorbed in prayer for long hours; and unable to take any more, they left the Holy House to rest a while; then they would find her later, still motionless in recollection and almost in ecstasy. How blissful was her great soul in contemplation of the lofty mysteries of the Incarnation of the Word and the Mary’s divine motherhood! How eloquent she found those poor walls within which the source of grace had been released!

In Pompei too, where she went with several sisters, it was as it had been in Loreto; since Mother Rosa was insatiably absorbed in prayer, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini and her companions would leave the shrine for some refreshment and later find the Mother still intently involved in conversing with Our Lady. She also went as a pilgrim to Oropa where she tried in vain to induce her brother Federico to make his confession, and to Lourdes, where she stayed for several days, most of which she spent praying prostrate on the ground.

Because of her infinite love for the Mother of God she considered that the Associations of the Daughters of Mary which existed then were the most beautiful flowers of the Institute, which is why she also wanted them on the missions, warmly recommended them to all her superiors, wished to be informed in detail about them, and rejoiced when she was told of the celebrations that had taken place in those pious unions.

Mary was a source of light and an incentive to Mother Rosa for the devotion to her holy mother, St. Anne; indeed, she habitually called her “Mother of the Immaculate”, recognizing this as the most honorable title for a woman so great, and she instilled such love for her in her sisters as to make a significant contribution to the spread of the devotion to St. Anne in the second half of the 19th century. Indeed, all the houses where Rosa Gattorno’s religious lived were as many centers for the devotion to the Holy Mother of Mary Immaculate, and the respective communities lived a way of life whose model was inspired by the family of St. Anne (cf. Const. Chap. 10).

Another visible fruit of Mother Rosa’s faith was her great love of worship and the decorum of churches.

In many of the Institute’s houses, bishops noted that no parish church was as well provided with sacred furnishings as the chapels of the Daughters of St. Anne. In Piacenza, Bishop Pellizzari, many years after Rosa Gattorno’s death, was amazed at the religious objects found in the chapel of the Mother House and said to the sisters: “Not even my cathedral is as well decorated as your church!”. Yet they were still all the same objects that dated back to the Mother’s time. Given the great poverty of the house, especially at the early stages of the Institute, some religious remarked that perhaps such splendor in church was excessive or at least out of place, but the Mother would answer “nothing is ever excessive for God”; indeed, she also made everyone work hard for the poor churches outside the Institute.

Rapture in contemplation of the mysteries of the Incarnation and the Redemption ~ What has been said will have clearly portrayed the style and interiority of this woman of faith. “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also”, Jesus said; Rosa Gattorno’s treasure consisted only in supernatural things, so it was for these alone that she strove. It is therefore not surprising that God rewarded such piety with extraordinary enlightenments.

When once she went to Messina for a visitation of the community, she entered the chapel as usual to adore the Blessed Sacrament. Since the sisters and those being instructed were praying together in the public church, on that occasion the chaplain had not celebrated in the house chapel and the tabernacle was empty. The superior, Sr. Anna Gonzaga Boeri, had nevertheless had the chapel and the altar prepared as though the Holy Eucharist were present and had even ensured that the candles and lamp were lit. The Mother knelt to pray; but soon rising to greet the sisters, she immediately turned to the superior and said to her: “How is it that you don’t have the Blessed Sacrament here?” She and the other members of the house were amazed that she knew the truth.

Likewise, in Piacenza she noticed without being told that the holy water stoup in the infirmary was filled with ordinary water, and called to order the sacristan who had been sure that this would have escaped her attention.17

In 1887, for the consecration of the church in Via Merulana, the Mother summoned Sr. Anna Ulderica Tazioli from Sicily to play the organ and rehearse the religious in singing the liturgy. As soon as she arrived, the sister was smitten with a fever and rheumatic pains so that she was unable to move and had to stay in bed. Despite this, the Mother gave the order for the sisters to go to choir practice; the sister replied that she was too stiff to move, and for that evening had arranged for another to replace her. But the following day, the Mother repeated her order: the sick sister, leaning with difficulty on the nurse, went to her study to convince her of her true state of health and inability to play the organ.

“Oh, how silly you are”, the Mother answered her, “to be worried about so little. Now you will come down to lunch with me, and you will see that you will be better”. At lunch she made her eat bean and pasta soup, boiled potatoes seasoned with olive oil and an egg, whereas until that moment the sick sister had not been able to take anything except a little milk.

After half an hour’s rest, she enjoined her to call the religious for choir practice; she obeyed, felt well and fulfilled her task with dignity: the memory of this famous event endured among the Daughters of St. Anne and was attested by several of them in their depositions at the processes.18

However, the Servant of God, seeing Sr. Anna Ulderica shortly afterwards, gave her this stern warning which is proof of the great faith which she wanted to inspire in her religious. “You see, Sr. Anna Ulderica, had you obeyed immediately, you would have been cured sooner!”.

At times she even wished them to live to the point of heroism this spirit of abandonment to the power of God, in which it is necessary to believe also in practical things, or otherwise — she maintained — one would not be responding fully to the great call to serve the Lord.

This is how Mother Gattorno taught the practice of faith. In 1880 she sent Sr. Anna Ancilla Briccoli to open a house of nurses in Pisa and established her there as superior. Discouraged by various difficulties, the sister wrote to the Mother after two months that “she would be content to be alive in purgatory rather than to be superior in that house”. The Foundress left her there for another two months; then she summoned her to Pistoia when she was passing through and, showing a hint of disapproval, said to her: “So you don’t want to go on being superior in Pisa? Well, this time I obey you; but mind, subsequently you will have to obey me”. And she immediately subjected her to a long, harsh trial, sending her to Palermo.

Although Sr. Anna Ancilla had requested an interview and gone to Naples for this purpose, the Mother did not grant her an audience nor did she speak to her for another ten days: then she sent her to Rome to wait in Vicolo del Piombo while she visited Palermo. On her return to Rome, she still did not want to receive her; so the sister wrote letters to her, staying in the same house and weeping because the Mother was pretending not to notice anything; indeed one day, showing her the waste-paper basket, the Mother said to her: “Do you see where your letters are?”. At a house celebration the Mother, surrounded by all the community, gave a small image to each religious except Sr. Anna Ancilla, who was even right beside her.

At last she sent her to the house in Spello, Umbria. Here the sisters greeted her as superior, while she herself knew nothing. Yet this was the case; the Mother General had announced that she was superior without telling her anything. Sr. Anna Ancilla was utterly astonished; she wrote three times protesting but had no answer. Finally a short letter came which said: “If you are superior, you are so because that is my will. Do well; I bless you in my crucified Christ”.

“In Spello”, Sr. Anna Ancilla concludes, “I resigned myself and no longer complained in my letters to the Mother about being superior”.19

Having seen that this religious had learned how to be obedient and to be detached from everything, she made her superior in several houses, and after a few years, in 1889, sent her as superior and visitor to Bolivia.

Faith put to the test and miraculous cures ~ Several times she demanded of other sisters a similar exercise of faith with total abandonment to obedience. She once ordered a novice, Sr. Anna Simeona, crippled by such obstinate arthritis that she had to be carried from her bed to the work room and could never join community meals, to go down stairs and walk about the house. This is how it happened. When the Mother had finished her lunch in the refectory, and it was her habit to be quick, she got up from the table and went upstairs to see the novice; asking her where she felt pain, she blessed her; then, as though remembering something she had forgotten, “Oh”, she exclaimed, “go downstairs to the office and have the secretary give you the purse I have left on my table”.

Sr. Anna Simeona, thinking only of carrying out the order she had received, got up from where she was sitting and prepared to go down to the office. At the top of the stairs, Mother Gattorno, who was watching her, ordered her to be quick. So she hurried downstairs and entered the office, asking for the Mother’s purse. The secretaries laughed at her request, but also wondered at seeing her standing on her own: “Don’t you realize that the Mother sent you downstairs to see how you walked? Don’t you realize you are better?”.

“But it’s true!”, exclaimed Sr. Anna Simeona”, “I feel no more pain”. And she never suffered from arthritis again.20

In the house at Cercola, a certain Sr. Anna Babila was seriously ill; the doctor had forbidden her to eat anything, considering it very dangerous, and allowed her only a little liquid. The sisters were watching over her by night because of her worrying condition. The Mother came from Naples to see her and stayed a while in her room alone with her; then she called the superior, had her brought the little lunch which had been prepared for the community since it was precisely midday, and urged the ill sister to eat. She trustingly obeyed; then she dressed herself in the Mother’s presence, and went to the community recreation with her, completely cured. The following day, at the Mother’s orders, she left for another destination.21

In Naples, at the house in Via Duomo, another sister was so ill that the priest was also watching by her side fearing that she would pass away from one moment to the next. One morning, the Mother who was in Naples for the visitation, went to see this sick sister; after a few minutes she asked her where her shoes were, and she answered in a faint voice that she did not know. The Mother then went out and asked the infirmarian where the sick woman’s clothes were; she was told that they had already taken everything away, thinking she would no longer need it. The Mother, however, wanted those things at once, helped the sick sister to dress, and then accompanied her to the chapel on the floor above, where the religious were gathered for meditation. They were astonished and almost frightened to see the sister they knew to be dying come in. The sister attended Holy Mass with the others and then, whether that same day or the next is not certain, left for Rome22.

These wonders worked by faith made the Mother’s heart rejoice deeply, for she saw in those docile souls the marvels of her Beloved; she knew very well that the Almighty is pleased to manifest himself where the creature does not set up the obstacle of distrust. We can say that the inspiration with which the Lord moved that great soul to such acts was certainly extraordinary; but he found in her the disposition of special gifts of the Spirit, and in those favored by grace, docility to the government of their Mother.

Wonderful facts like these are countless in the sworn depositions of the processes and in the handwritten Memoirs of various religious of the Institute; they took place at very different times and places and, at least in most cases, in people of normal temperament. They are therefore a clear testimony to Mother Rosa’s rock-solid faith and to the school in which she trained her Daughters. She urged the superiors never to take any decision impulsively without first having prayed a great deal before the Crucifix, since their government had to rest on God’s light.

Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini relates of herself that she received this advice from the Foundress when, still young, she was assigned to the mission in America with the office of Provincial. She always kept to it and then immediately informed the Mother of the decisions taken. But then it became clear that the Crucifix was also for the Mother a source of extraordinary light to know distant things according to the needs of her government. For while a letter from Valentini was traveling from America to Europe, another from Mother Gattorno was coming from Europe to America with these or similar words: “I know you have decided such and such: you have done very well”. And this without anyone having been able to inform the Mother beforehand.

Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini concludes: “This happened to me many times”23.

All who knew Mother Rosa, lay people and priests, members of her Institute and outsiders, agree in emphasizing her keenness of mind and the shrewdness of her government. That she had great wisdom there is no doubt; but we are certain that this could not have sufficed for all that this admirable woman accomplished. In certain souls God kindles another light, making their intellect share in knowledge and judgments proper to a higher wisdom; and so he did with this servant of his.

He gave her “very great wisdom, discernment, and breadth of understanding as vast as the sand on the seashore” (1 Kgs 5:9).

The desire to remain in the shade — Radical poverty and total self-emptying — Unlimited trust in God and the deep desire for supernatural gifts — Divine favors obtained with prayer and penance — Pedagogical support to encourage growth in the faith.

The desire to remain in the shade ~ “I would like to go to paradise at all costs and to take all my daughters there”.1 Words like these, so ardent and determined, were often on the Mother’s lips, especially when she was reproving or comforting one of her sisters, as if to define her objective and to fire them with enthusiasm in the will to reach the goal.

Her work was nothing else than striving with all her might for the spiritual good of souls, an obvious sign that she was clearly aware of that good, held it in supreme esteem and had an immense love for it. In her thirty-four years of religious life she had accepted and formed thousands of souls in her Institute and opened hundreds of houses on several continents, in which the sisters worked every day as in Christ’s vineyard. Looking at it in this light, Mother Rosa’s life seems really active and fruitful.

We have already spoken several times of the great charge of enthusiasm and vitality that Rosa Gattorno brought to her new apostolic undertakings; here it is necessary to describe in greater detail the line of conduct she followed for herself in pursuing the aims for which she yearned. In fact there are many who aspire to heaven and also to the virtues required to enter it, but those who take the difficult narrow paths that lead to that goal are few. St. Augustine says that one must start with profound humility: “Are you thinking of building a very tall building? First think of founding it on humility”.2 Mother Rosa considered humility so essential as to be a great treasure to be guarded with jealous care.

In her writings she frequently says that she learned precious lessons about humility from prayer, precisely as an indispensable condition for possessing the kingdom of God. “He made me aware of how much he loves this beautiful virtue and that one can have all the greatest qualities of the world, but without humility one cannot possess his kingdom” (M. 2, p. 94).

As a faithful disciple of this doctrine, she constantly sought to avoid praise and detested even the signs of esteem for her shown by her Daughters

Her first secretary, Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino, studiously noted every event that she considered extraordinary and all that she observed in the Foundress’ clear and irreprehensible attitude, certain of pleasing the sisters of the future. After several years, the Mother found these writings by chance and made her disgust quite plain.

She also expressed great annoyance to another beloved daughter who was close to her and displayed interest in her every gesture, giving the impression that she virtually wanted to investigate the affairs of the soul of the Mother who reprimanded her several times, saying that she did not know how to put up with her. This effort to divert attention from herself was so sincere and habitual that those outside the Institute who came into contact with her found it supremely edifying.

“Your Mother is holy through her great humility”, said the Franciscan Friar Angelo to a Daughter of St. Anne.3

One year, on a visitation to the houses in Sicily, she went to see Cardinal Dusmet in Catania; she had a long somewhat stormy discussion with him that ended with the withdrawal of the Daughters of St. Anne from one house. But the Prelate was amazed by the Mother’s conduct. “I was edified”, he said later to the provincial, Sr. Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, “by your Mother’s humility and submission because regarding what I said to her, and I certainly had much to say, she took everything in holy peace”.4

Not only did she show displeasure at being called Mother General by her Daughters, but because of her longing to be in the shade and attend to her soul with greater recollection, she tried several times to relinquish this office.

She made a first attempt at the Chapter of 1881, but met with staunch and unanimous opposition in all the sisters assembled and in Bishop Scalabrini who was presiding at the Chapter.5 She repeated this act several times and even managed to gather the whole community including the novices, as Sr. Anna Cunegonda Pacini testified, begging on her knees to be exonerated from her office.6

She reiterated her plea at the private Chapter in 1886, the first to be held in Rome; but as on former occasions she was again unanimously voted for. At last it came to the ears of Leo XIII who, at an audience he granted to her with Mother Carrega, dissuaded her from the very thought of relinquishing her office and said to her: “Ah no, no! On the contrary we appoint you General for life!”.7

The Mother bowed her head and insisted no more; at the subsequent General Chapters her office was no longer voted for, but she said to some sisters that it was only obedience that kept her in it.8

All her religious nonetheless saw clearly how she was reacting and were moved to wonder; for not only did she lower herself to do the humblest services to the sick whom she unfailingly visited with great affection, but she sometimes served in the kitchen too, preparing food, serving out the portions and kneading the bread.

Radical poverty and total self-emptying ~ She wanted the furnishings in her room and the small study in which she received people and worked to be particularly simple and very poor: a small table, two chairs and a crucifix were the only furniture. Only in her last years did she come round to permitting a rug to be put on the floor, because of the keen insistence of the general secretary who considered that this might prevent her health, already very precarious, from deteriorating. In her bedroom, she had only a straw pallet on an iron bedstead, with a pillow stuffed with straw, no mattress and no sheets; she slept in her clothes, wrapped in two black shawls. And this was all that the houses expecting her for a visitation needed to prepare. She took the two black shawls with her.9

It was the same with her clothes: she wanted nothing new and enjoyed wearing a very clean but rather worn habit that was even patched. Once she was given a new overall; she called Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza and said to her: “Give this to the cook to wear for a while, and then I shall wear it”.10 However, she agreed on one exception to this: that is, she had one habit in good condition that was not patched which she kept for visits to the Pope: she called it “the Pope’s dress”. However, with time even this ceased to be beautiful, for when she died not even “the Pope’s dress” was found to be decent for her to wear, but it had to do because there was nothing better.11

To wash herself she would only use the soap for the laundry, a common practice the Institute. She did all this not only for mortification, but through a deep sense of humility; and the sentiment lived on the Institute after her death.

She gave frequent signs of this self-emptying in the various communities she visited, tactfully adjusting to the common timetable and the measures of the local superiors. Sometimes she would present herself saying that she was a poor dunce who did not understand a thing and knew nothing; among them she would learn something. Moreover, from her crucified Christ she would learn everything.

Since her works were sometimes praised, especially in the last decade of her life when the Institute’s great flourishing in Italy and abroad astounded even the most important personages and was highly praised in the houses, she promptly replied that it had nothing to do with her, since the Work was God’s.

In Chapter XIII we have already told how she managed to transform the Duchess of Sorrentino from a lady with a life of worldly refinement into a religious, for she became a Daughter of St. Anne in 1892.

The aspect that most impressed Sr. Anna Maria Teresa Patti di Sorrentino was precisely the great humility of the Mother who constantly deprecated her own work. “I am a miserable creature”, she wrote, “capable of nothing; everything is imperfection me, only God’s mercy can make up for my wretchedness”. And in another letter: “Oh, how clear it is that charity done by me is never well done! I feel profound sorrow […] at having harmed the Lord’s Work”. And again, “On this earth only work and suffering must be my daily bread. I have sinned frequently and am always an abyss of wickedness; this is why everything must painful to me; but I am lucky enough to love suffering, and find my delight in that alone”.12

With these sincere sentiments she exercised her authority: she was firm in her measures and strong in governance, but gave no sign of arrogance, not even with sisters who were less compliant. On the contrary, to some who were closer to her, she would say in her last years that they ought to have another General, since she had spoiled the Lord’s Work.13

Unlimited trust in God and the deep desire for supernatural gifts ~ We have lingered in pointing out Mother Gattorno’s deep humility, wishing instead to speak of her heroic hope; indeed, precisely this aspect of Mother Rosa’s spirituality must be illustrated in order to grasp the true nature and correct degree of her hope. Few people, it seems to us, are aware that it is only in humility that the necessary foundation of trust in God exists. Indeed, many confuse Christian hope with simple belief in divine omnipotence and the divine promises; but they do not realize that total confidence in God presupposes the true sense of their own smallness, and the awareness that all their esteem and exaggerated attachment to their own person and every calculation are nothing but trappings; the pure, strong desire for supernatural gifts which is the true object of Christian hope is still necessary. Otherwise, instead of authentic hope one has crude recklessness or complacent egoism. Rosa Gattorno, in her sincere and total self-emptying, prepared the proper atmosphere of theological hope and drew from a most intense love of divine things the dynamism for the great undertakings which made her life a luminous page in the Church’s history.

The first fruits of Mother Rosa’s boundless hope can be seen in herself, since the Lord rewarded so great an abandonment in him by giving her extraordinary gifts and immense energy in the work of governance, even at an advanced age. When one thinks of her almost 34 years as Mother General among so many concerns and trials in more than 360 foundations since the birth of the Institute, and even more, if one considers her method of governance in which she wanted to reach personally almost everywhere, we are presented with a task so great that the ordinary energies of even a most robust person would not seem to suffice. Yet she was equal to it, with her ailing body and formidable penances. “None of us”, says a religious who was very close to her, “could possibly compete with her stamina”.14

Her lofty serenity when coping with so much was a cause of wonder: “Sometimes”, Mother Celsa Speranza tells, “looking at the difficulties the Institute encountered in the early years when I was working in the office, I would say to the Servant of God: But Mother, when you go to bed you will not be able to sleep! ‘Oh no, daughter’, she would answer me, ‘when I retire to my room in the evening, I think for two minutes, then I turn to my crucified Christ and tell him: I have done everything I could and to the best of my ability; you see to your Work now. Then I place everything at the feet of my crucified Christ and I don’t think about it any longer, as though the Work did not exist’. And I also heard her repeat this to various superiors”.15

“Several times”, said another sister, “in seeing her fired at from all sides and betrayed by persons she had helped, I asked her how she could possibly continue to trust in the human race; and the Servant of God answered me: ‘I trust in my Jesus and enough’”.16 that is

What she felt, she taught. She recommended those who went to see her in the most difficult situations first of all to detach themselves from their own will and to put themselves back in the Lord’s hands as a useful instrument, expecting every good thing from him. “Try to take everything to the feet of Jesus crucified; he will repair everything and will give you peace and comfort in the adversities of this miserable life”.17

“The less we are involved with ourselves, the more we will find ourselves in God; if we work for the earth, only the earth will bear fruits, and they will never be good for the Lord”.

These were not empty repetitions of what saints had said, but words that welled up from her spirit, accompanied by the wonderful effectiveness of her example to spur her Daughters towards the great conquests. For this reason the Mother’s open fondness of hardships and privations in her own life deserve to be emphasized; that is, they are the basis of the practice of trust in God. The difficulties that she encountered, particularly in the early days of the foundation, made her certain that it was a work of God; and several times she was heard to say: “If I were to see the Institute prospering, I should be afraid because it would appear to me that it was not a work of the Lord. The more troubled I see it, the more certain I am that the work is truly God’s”.18

Divine favors obtained with prayer and penance ~ In these difficulties, her way of praying and of having prayers said became particularly fervent. She ordered the exposition of the Blessed Sacrament and sent the sisters in turn for adoration; she herself spent long hours in chapel, freeing herself from every commitment. But, from a sentence that escaped her once when she was at the bedside of one of her religious who was seriously ill, we know that she habitually added harsh penances in difficult cases. “When a grace is difficult to obtain”, she said, “I offer the Lord something very painful; after which he has never denied me whatever I have asked him”.19

In spring 1898, on her last journey to Sicily, she took her granddaughter, Maria Barbiellini with her. In Palermo the girl caught a virulent typhus, which in two weeks brought her close to death, as the doctor declared.

The Mother was very distressed about her; she recommended all the sisters to pray and she herself spent the whole night in front of the tabernacle. Thinking she was alone, she sometimes prayed aloud, addressing St Anne with groans, and every now and then she was silent, as though listening. Towards morning she stood up and left the chapel serene: she knew she had been heard with regard to her granddaughter’s cure,20 as in fact was the case.

However her absolute trust in God’s goodness did not hinder her in the activity which must accompany the fulfilment of great desires, and it prompted her to call on the blessed intercessors for help, especially the Patrons of the Institute. Entirely dedicated as they were to works of charity and in some institutions to abandoned persons, the religious always had to keep their gaze on Providence, the only reliable source of help for immediate needs. The Mother, however, did not want them to expect this help only from prayer, remaining inactive, but from serving God generously and constantly; so poverty had to be an incentive to observance of the Rule. For this reason she frequently put the superiors to the test.

In 1891, she sent Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini as Superior to Bassano, telling her: “I am sending you to a poor house; but if you have faith, Providence will not fail you”. The sister found greater poverty in Bassano than she had expected; the house lacked everything and was also burdened with debts left by a sick superior. There were taxes to pay but they did not have even a penny. In addition, a few days after Sr. Anna Camilla’s arrival, an earthquake caused the surrounding wall to collapse; it had to be rebuilt immediately so as not to leave the house open to all and sundry. The situation was more critical than ever: what solution could there be? Sr. Anna Camilla saw there was no money and did not know where to find some; so she asked the Mother General but quickly realized she had taken the wrong step. After a few days in fact, the Mother sent her another little girl to look after, writing to her: “She is three-years old, she was highly recommended to me; train her well for me, because in time she will yield her fruits”. The superior understood. The humane act was accompanied by the prayers of the thirty children in their care and the twenty sisters, most of whom were elderly and ill, and Providence did not fail them. Discreet sums of money arrived and twenty quintals of wheat which had to be stored in rented premises because they had no granary; then more and more letters containing alms, but anonymous. A young bride, a former pupil, even came to Bassano from Bolivia where Sr. Anna Camilla had been a missionary, and left her some good Bolivians. The aid of Providence flowed in constantly, so that in four years the house was renewed throughout, indeed it was enlarged and furnished. However, the loveliest conclusion was that Sr. Anna Camilla asked the Mother’s forgiveness for the meagre faith she had had, or rather for not having really understood previously what faith in Providence means; yet on other occasions she had had illuminating lessons on the subject, as has been said in Chapter XV.21

Pedagogical support to encourage growth in the faith ~ Mother Rosa continued this form of educational guidance in the letters to the superiors. To ensure that the secretaries had properly interpreted her creative concept of authentic hope, she had the letters they had written brought to her and had the diligence to read them all before sending them.

Even more than poverty, Mother Rosa’s tenacious hope is demonstrated by the many serious tribulations that afflicted her throughout her life. The Christian flavor of earthly life is precisely in this exercise, as the Apostle Paul says: “But that is not all we can boast about; we can boast about our sufferings. These sufferings bring patience, as we know, and patience brings perseverance and perseverance brings hope, and this hope is not deceptive because the love of God has been poured into our hearts…” (Rom 5:3-5).

Indeed, tribulations are the sign of Christ who entered into his glory through them.

Therefore, closely united to Christ, Mother Gattorno bore the weight of adversity with wonderful great-heartedness for long years.

Her constant courage, peaceful goodness and freshness in all her governance while she had to fight every kind of enemy and adversity were the fruit of an arcane inner strength which she drew from the deep certainty that God would help her, because she served him with simplicity of heart. The solemn depositions of the Processes abound with uniform judgments like these: “I have never seen a soul as resigned to the Lord’s will as our Mother. We were often amazed to see the tranquillity with which she bore not only physical sufferings, which she took no account of at all, but also moral ones, of which there were so many”22.

Thus, anchored to her Crucifix, this most faithful disciple of the saving Word held firm to the very end, when an even more frightening storm seemed to shake her and the Institute; perhaps God wished her to close her life with a supreme trial, so that her hope might reach the height of heroism. In the last days of her life she exclaimed: “I have finished suffering: the Institute will triumph”23.

In fact, the Apostolic Visitation closed a few years later with a substantially positive outcome; all the Provinces of the Daughters of St. Anne drew new vigor from it and spread to other mission lands as far as the East.

Intense communion with her Good — An episode in the Rome Novitiate — Her Good, lover and beloved above all things — Motionless absorption during thanksgiving at Communion — Devotion to the Heart of Christ — A conversion at Foligno — Love extended also to the souls of the deceased — An agonizing desire to see God.

Intense communion with her Good ~ no life can be genuinely Christian unless it is imbued with a pure love of God and consequently of neighbor; and Rosa Gattorno’s life really was a heroic poem of love. What has been told here is no more than the development of the splendid adventure of a soul that let itself be fashioned by the bright reflections of the immense blaze kindled on earth by the Son of the Father, who loved to the point of supreme sacrifice. All that now remains is to gather the precious gleanings from so abundant a harvest.

Christ gave us an unmistakable sign of sincere love: “If you keep my commandments you will remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love” (Jn 15:10).

At the same time he notes how there can be different levels in this obedience, since he suggests himself as a supreme model of abandonment to the Father’s will. Now it is comforting to find people in Christ’s Church who understood this teaching so well that they make their own life an act of trusting abandonment. It seems to us that Rosa Gattorno has a most praiseworthy place among these privileged people.

Testimonies abound which document the integrity and transparency of the Mother’s life and her extreme delicacy of conscience, which sometimes verges on punctiliousness. In her conferences to the religious she insisted that they take care to avoid even the slightest shortcoming or offense to God. Indeed, she was most distressed when she came to know that in some house mutual respect was lacking and that the sisters were saying nasty things behind one another’s backs; she insisted relentlessly that forgiveness be asked of the person maligned.1

The very thought of an offense to God filled her with sorrow and at public events where she knew irreverent voices would be raised, as often occurred in those times, she sought every possible means to atone for them in some way with various proofs of love. Thus on the occasion of subversive meetings she would have the Blessed Sacrament exposed in chapel and desired all the sisters to take turns in adoration.2

This love for God and his law made her repeat: “If I knew that sin had entered the Lord’s Work, I should die of grief!”. She was certainly speaking of serious sin and the habit of it since she knew very well that human nature is also present with its weaknesses and incoherence in religious life. However, such sentiments prove how alert and vigilant her spirit was to any hint from the divine will. “She was”, they say, “strict in demanding observance, and did not give way to compromises”. Nonetheless it should be noted that she was the first to set the example, irreproachable in her behavior and unflagging in her work, despite her sufferings. It is a fact that sometimes the pallor of her face disclosed that she was ailing, but she dissembled it and continued to work as though nothing were the matter.3

There is no doubt that Mother Rosa was dominated by a tormented nostalgia for loftiness, an irrepressible desire for transparency, for the most intense communion with her Good, which is why she also abandoned herself to his mystery with the ingenuity and simplicity of little ones who alone are given to “know” by penetrating the opacity of events. These spiritual inclinations had long existed in Rosa: she decided to found the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne only through obedience to God’s will to which she was determined to adhere, despite the breaking of her mother’s heart which the sacrifice of her children would inevitably bring. It was a supreme act of love for God, sought above all else, even what was dearest to her on earth. One can certainly say that from that day she progressed with giant’s strides on the way of perfection.

Her heart was so full of love that she could not prevent it from brimming over and speaking of it, often with such emotion as to literally entrance those she was addressing.

Christ’s love in her was so overwhelming as to become the torch with which she illumined minds.

An episode in the Rome Novitiate ~ A rather marvellous event once occurred. Sr. Anna Cunegonda Pacini who still remembered that it was a Thursday, tells that one day in 1890, Mother Rosa went upstairs to visit the novices in the Generalate in Rome, when their Mistress was absent. She offered to give them a short talk, and asked them what they wanted her to speak about. “Oh, speak to us about the love of God!”, chorused the young girls. The Mother first tried to put them off, telling them it was a subject rather for Seraphim, but since they were so insistent she tackled the topic and almost immediately with such feeling that the novices were spellbound. She was speaking on a dais, standing in front of a bare table, as the Novice Mistress did; the large group of novices had clustered closely round her. Now she was so on fire speaking of the love of God that a rapid river of words flowed from her lips. Suddenly one of the novices caught the attention of her neighbor, Sr. Anna Cunegonda, and pointed out that the Mother had risen from the floor of the dais; indeed, approaching her and stretching out her hand, she noticed that she was about a hand’s breadth above the floor.

The news instantly rippled through the auditorium and all the novices looked at her in wonder; then succumbing to great emotion they fell to their knees, fixing their eyes, damp with tears, on the Mother who continued to speak in that position above the ground for almost half an hour and was certainly oblivious of the novices’ movements.4

Her Good, lover and beloved above all things ~ Already since early childhood, according to the testimonies, she had been heard to melt into ardent sighs of love for God whom she considered “lover” and “beloved” above all things. Nor was this sterile sentimentalism, as from that time Rosa was more committed to loving with generous deeds than with words, perhaps led to this by her solid and practical Genoese temperament, so far removed from vain sentimentalism. At home her mortifications had been somewhat closely controlled, but perhaps one had escaped attention. In seeing her abstaining from eating meat, no one suspected that she had a special liking for salumi, since as a little girl, as she herself recounted later, she would go to the family larder, cut slices of salami and eat them with pleasure.

Now it was precisely in privations of this kind that she found opportunities, arduous as they were humble, to demonstrate to God the strength of her love for him; for throughout her life, from childhood, she denied herself this food, yet lavished it upon others. Indeed, on the eve of the great solemnities she was accustomed to distributing to the poor a large quantity of pasta and sausages, and she would make the community serve similar dishes from time to time; then she would go into the kitchen and slice the sausages, thus tempting her former desire with their smell, but never tasting them.5

Likewise when she passed by grocers’ shops she would feel a longing for those foods, as she one day confessed to a sister whom she tried to convince that her abstinence from meat was not a penance, but a need dictated by her health. Through the association of ideas, David’s generous sacrifice springs to mind when, burning with thirst on the battlefield, he pours out on the ground the fresh water brought to him by the kind soldiers who had fetched it from the well at Bethlehem: “But David would drink none of it and poured it out as a libation to Yahweh” (1 Ch 11:18). How often did Mother Rosa repeat this act in more than fifty years!

Motionless absorption during thanksgiving at Communion ~ Bearing the seal of his martyrdom of love so deeply impressed upon her heart and her members, that most generous woman entered into her conversations with her Good with trust and fresh energy; however, she did not always succeed in hiding her inner fire, especially in front of the Blessed Sacrament. When night had fallen, while everything was wrapped in silence, she liked to go on a spiritual pilgrimage to all the houses of the Institute, adoring Jesus in the Sacrament in every tabernacle and repaying him with full affection for his immense condescension in dwelling under the humble roofs of her religious. Then she exacted from them every possible delicate attention for the divine guest; having seen a sacristan sister who, her tasks completed, was about to leave the church without spending a little time in adoration, she called her and in a friendly way made her see how improper this was, suggesting that she recite at least three Gloria Patris before leaving. She urged her sisters to receive Communion daily, but on condition that they spent ample time in preparation and thanksgiving for it.

She herself would remain giving thanks for about an hour, kneeling on the floor, leaning on the arm of a chair; she would stay there motionless and no one was allowed to call her during that time, for any reason. She was so deeply absorbed moreover, that no one would have dared to disturb her. Once the Bishop of La Paz in Bolivia came to celebrate Mass in the chapel of the Generalate in Rome, and Mother Gattorno and the other religious received Holy Communion from his hands. In Bolivia it was the custom for the celebrant, after the concluding prayer, to bring the lectionary to be kissed to the person for whom the holy sacrifice had been offered. The Bishop’s assistant therefore took the lectionary over to her but was unable to rouse her from her absorption; consequently the Bishop himself signalled to him not to insist.6

This motionless absorption before the Most Holy Eucharist was a habit of hers even when she was ill and until the end of her life; She would answer those who asked her what she could possibly find to say in such long hours: “Before Jesus, time has no time”.7

Devotion to the Heart of Christ ~ One would obviously suppose that in this profound intimacy Mother Gattorno would have had a conscious and fervent devotion to the Heart of Christ; such a soul could not fail to have the devotion of love par excellence. In fact, we know from reliable testimonies that she made it the fulcrum of her spiritual life and used it in directing her religious to perfection. “Why”, she said to someone, “don’t you run to the Heart of Jesus? — It is there that you will find true comfort and obtain graces to continue on the Lord’s path”.8

Absorbed in that most Sacred Heart she felt and wrote not literary, but passionate and lucid pages on the interior life. In the fragment of a reflection written in Cento on 2 May 1867 that has been left to us, we read a beautiful conversation with Jesus about the way to enter his most Sacred Heart. “First”, the Lord said to her, “you must look at me and know that whoever [wants] to enter here must [suffer] these torments […]. It is not enough, my beloved, to meditate on these sufferings of mine if you do not come to feel their pain with me; and you must taste this suffering with peace, resignation, pleasure and love […], if you do this, full permission [to enter] will be granted to you, and to live for ever in this grotto of love in my side”. Rosa’s answer was prompt and lasted all her life, as we have seen, in a heroic sacrifice of herself: “To be mine, all mine, from now on […] the thoughts of your bride will be of nothing other than suffering, doing whatever will please you and the Father”.9

In that grotto of love, she not only experienced physical suffering but was also involved in total immolation of the spirit; her zeal for the conversion of sinners enflamed her to the point of agony, and several sisters describe the heartfelt tones in which she spoke on this topic.10

From that divine Heart, the source of infinite love, she drew the norm and measure of her relations with others, all of whose miseries she wanted to relieve so that she could take them all as a burden upon herself, in the image of the Savior. The Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne was conceived by her in a living impulse of love and was entirely dedicated to assistance of the poor, the lowliest, the oppressed, the defenseless, the abandoned.

Dominated by her passion for the divine and the human, she made a total investment of her life, suffering anguish for the kingdom and accepted without any mitigation the radical and involving requirements of the Gospel. Therefore her preferential options were mainly for the situations of risk in which innocents in particular might be involved and overwhelmed by evil.

A conversion at Foligno ~ From a deposition of Canon Pietro Tosti of Foligno we know that in 1873, just after the house of the Daughters of St. Anne had been opened in that city, Mother Rosa was invited to visit a seriously ill young man, the victim of his vices and so hostile to religion as to have himself guarded by two friends to ensure that no priest approached him. On the first nights the Mother limited herself to healing the body of the sick young man in order to win his soul, but at the appropriate moment she spoke to him so effectively of the spiritual life and of the eternal reward that he expressed the desire to make his confession and prepared himself very well, frequently asking to kiss the crucifix. But how could a priest approach him? Mother Rosa knew from this same young man that his friends would not leave until one or two o’clock in the morning. So she made the proper arrangements with the parish priest of the cathedral, let him in to the sick young man at that hour and he confessed with deep and heartfelt joy, exclaiming: “Now I am happy!”. And he wanted again and again to kiss the crucifix which the Mother kept with her constantly. He therefore decided to dismiss his guards saying that now he had that lady’s assistance he no longer required their offices. They realized that some religious change had occurred in the companion of their secret society and sought revenge. So they lay in wait for the Mother one morning, when she was leaving that house to go to Mass in the cathedral at about five o’clock; one of them attacked her with a dagger, but with a scream she managed to escape, leaving the rascal disappointed, for he was not brave enough to run after her and finish her off.

However, a few days later, the Mother was summoned by a city magistrate and urged to leave Foligno, since her work there was so disliked by the people as to incur these attacks. “I would understand”, she replied with her habitual calm, “such a measure were I doing evil; but if I do good it is also natural that I have to suffer a bit”.

The magistrate did not insist and she was able to remain and to continue her charitable mission.11

This indomitable love for souls also impelled her to go to the bedside of persons who were particularly hostile to her, to assist them with delicate love and bring them the balm of divine comforts, especially when it was a matter of some priest or other who had failed in his duties to his vocation; so that neither life’s dangers nor wounds to her self-esteem could extinguish that resplendent flame of love.12

This was the lesson she also imparted to her religious. “When you come across a sick person”, she would say, “who does not ask for the sacraments, do not waste yourself in words, but do everything for him in such a way as to elicit admiration; visit him often so as to discover his wishes and you will see that he himself will ask for the sacraments”. And this is what often happened; many Daughters of St. Anne were exultant as they told of the good results obtained by following these norms and the example of their Foundress: “Where have you learned such love? Who taught you? Not even my mother and my sister have done so much”. These and similar words were spoken by the sick in the hospital of Borgo San Donnino (today Fidenza) to the superior, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini; and since she replied that it was required by Christian charity, they started thinking on new lines. In that hospital an atheist doctor and administrator were converted to God; in four years, all the patients except for one received the comforts of religion.13 Obviously all this was a cause of great joy to the Mother.

Love extended also to the souls of the deceased ~ Her compassion was not limited to the suffering of this life; she extended it to the souls in need of help in purgatory, remembering that the living members of Christ’s mystical Body must share sincerely in the sufferings of all its members. Therefore in addition to the many prayers of suffrage for the Institute’s deceased members, she also wanted to offer prayers for all the dead; indeed, on various occasions she was heard to exclaim: “Oh, if only I could get enough money together to assure a daily Mass in our church for the souls in purgatory, how happy I would be!”. She succeeded, establishing the necessary funds for a daily Mass and two on Sundays; in addition she kept for the chapel in the Generalate a daily collection to pay for Mass in suffrage for the souls in Purgatory.14

Then on All Souls’ Day she invited as many priests as possible to celebrate the Mass of suffrage in the church in Rome. With motherly finesse she anticipated the desires of her religious whenever they were afflicted by some bereavement, giving the poorest ones money to have Mass celebrated wherever they wished.15

It is not surprising therefore that God rewarded such concern by occasionally revealing to her the state of some soul already passed on to the next world. In her writings the Mother herself tells of many apparitions concerning dead people. Sr. Anna Geronima Mazza tells us of an event that she herself witnessed.

The house of the Daughters of St. Anne in Pistoia was offered to the Institute by an elderly canon who, however, continued to live in it until his death. Given his advanced age and illness, he had an old serving woman with whom he did not always agree, so that every now and then the house echoed with their squabbles and shouting and the superior would come down from the floor of the religious to make peace in their little flat.

Three months after the canon’s death, Mother Gattorno had to pass through Pistoia and stayed there for three days. On the last day she was seen in chapel absorbed in prayer before the image of the Sacred Heart, kneeling and resting her arm on a chair as usual. The superior who needed to speak to her called her gently, but to no avail; she shook her repeatedly, but in vain; then she withdrew, going to complain to the secretary. After some time the Mother went to her room and summoned her, but seemed strangely preoccupied; she made her sit down beside her, then taking her hand, she took her to the chapel and made her kneel by the chair she had used to lean on. They remained in silence for a while; then the Mother asked the sister:

“Geronima, do you hear that voice?”.

“Yes, I do, Mother”.

“Whose is that voice? Do you recognize it?”.

“Mother, it is Canon Biagini’s voice”.

The sister had in fact recognized the voice heard so often in the quarrels on the floor below; the priest’s room had been directly under the chapel.

“Do not be afraid, Geronima”, the Mother added, taking her by the hand; she brought her back to her room, had her sit down, and remained a while in silence. Then she continued: “Geronima, you recognized the voice of Canon Biagini; he is saved but if you knew or saw his serious sufferings in purgatory and how he has to pay with the restlessness of his spirit for the Masses celebrated, you would never cease to pray for him for the rest of your life”. She also said that the canon had been saved because of the way he had benefited the Institute and through the intercession of St. Anne. “Have Masses celebrated”, the Foundress concluded, “recite Rosaries and pray, pray a lot for this soul”.16

These were the nuances of Mother Rosa’s love; there was no suffering or privation in which she did not share. Her interest and passion for the glory of God intensified her commitment beyond the limits of earthly life, after having given everything and herself for the immense poverty and miseries of humanity. She wanted the image of the Creator to be restored to everyone so that they would all sing of his glory.

An agonizing desire to see God ~ However, Rosa felt and measured the torment of souls in Purgatory in her own desire to see God. In another fragment of her private writings found after her death we read these words: “Come on! For pity’s sake let me see you, you who have robbed me of my heart! My breast is wounded with your love! […]. Ah, what sorrows are these! They can be called a purgatory on earth! And you, poor souls, whatever can I give you? Lord, my Beloved, my All, if you see something in me that can be of use to these souls, ah, take from them that cloud which makes them suffer so…”. And immediately thinking of her arrival in eternity she adds: “My dear Good, grant that I do not have to enter that purgatory, yes […] so that I can immediately clasp your feet […]. Tell me so, my Good, for I am dying of love”.17

To see God is the agonizing desire of those who live in perfect love; and on earth this love is a real anticipation of future life because, lacking all the necessary virtues for the fulfilment of good works, it will remain eternally as a glorious bond of the creature with God, a sublime likeness of him who is infinite Love. For this precise reason Mother Rosa yearned for heaven, while she jealously guarded the lamp destined to shine in the procession of the divine Bridegroom: “Oh, how beautiful heaven is!”, she exclaimed, “when will we get there?”18.
