(1894-1898) Journey to Sicily: a house for the Novitiate in Palermo; the opening of another seven houses — New foundations — Further expeditions to Africa — New claims and provocations of Mother Rosa’s son-in-law — Last journey to Sicily — Spiritual testament (30 August 1898) — Deterioration of health — Last reminder to the novices and definitive departure from Piacenza.

Journey to Sicily: a house for the Novitiate in Palermo; the opening of another seven houses ~ What with the desire to see God and the commitment to procure his glory tirelessly, the great evening had now come for Mother Rosa; her radiant days on earth were fading into the gleams of an equally luminous twilight. In 1872, it had seemed to her that her goal was already at hand; instead, a fruitful and hardworking period in her life still lay ahead.1

After the definitive approval of the Rule, she had seen the Institute develop rapidly with new vitality in Italy, America and Africa, but all this involved greater efforts although she was coming to that time in life known today as “the age of retirement”. Her unconditional giving to the very end also deeply moved external persons who came to her for advice and comfort, well aware of the sacrifice she must have to bear; so Princess Odescalchi, asking the secretaries for news of her, would say “How is your crucified Mother? Your Mother really is crucified!”.2

In the meantime, her strength was noticeably waning, so that after 1894 she was obliged to make a few changes in the rigorous diet she had stuck to until then; but it required an order from the Cardinal Protector, after the doctor had expressed his opinion; she then became used to eating eggs and dairy products and drinking a little wine.3 However, she continued to abstain from any kind of dessert, even when she offered some to the community.

That year 1894 was particularly busy. During the month of January she made a journey to Sicily to visit the many houses there, although the island at the time was troubled by seditious movements founded by subversives; it seemed that God was opening up to her the paths to new foundations with special generosity. In fact, in Palermo, through the Princess di Fitalia’s munificence, she purchased the house for the novitiate in Sicily and for a boarding school for children of the nobility in Via d’Ossuna. The negotiations for that most important house had been going on for some time: the princess longed for a grand foundation from the start and was willing to rent a large group of buildings should her means be insufficient for an immediate purchase; instead, the Mother, now fortified by her experience, directed things in more modest, safer ways, which can be compared to the mustard seed. She preferred a smaller house that could be enlarged later when the Work had taken root. This was the best solution as events were shortly to prove.4

During her stay on the island and during the return journey to Rome, the tireless Mother opened another seven houses of the Institute, many of which had a certain importance: the home for beggars in Sambuca, the hospital at Corleone, a nursery school in Dongo and another, the “Duchessa Ravaschieri”, in Naples, the Conservatorio delle Pentite (home for former prostitutes) in Messina, the female prison in Bari, and the beggars’ home in Rossano.

New foundations ~ On her return to Rome in May she saw to other foundations, such as those in Nizza Marittima and in Manaus, Brazil, while the many clothings of novices in the Generalate opened her heart to new hopes. In July she set out once again for Pisa, Sampierdarena and Piacenza. Nothing impeded her energetic governance, which was always intended not only to intensify the charitable work, but also to promote fidelity to the observance of the Rule. She was opposed to those exclusive friendships which impoverish a community and prevent its openness and apostolic dynamism, and which can easily spring up also between religious and lay people; therefore on this occasion she transferred many sisters and superiors, restoring peace, freshness and vigor to the communities.

In the autumn she opened another nine houses so that in 1894 nineteen had been opened. This was the brightening glow of a flame that was dying.

In the meantime she also lent a hand to another very important work. The public church dedicated to “Mary Mater Gratiae”, next door to the Generalate, had been designed in such a way that it was somewhat low and airless, uncomfortable for the people who often flocked to it. Mother Rosa improved its conditions, on a design by the engineer Bencivegna. The work lasted for about a year and involved heavy costs; the church was reopened to the public in May 1895.

Further expeditions to Africa ~ That year was particularly important for missionary action in Eritrea, where the Daughters of St. Anne, who had been in Africa since 1886, took over all the houses formerly directed by the Daughters of Charity who had been obliged to leave the territory. Cardinal Ledochowski, the Prefect of the Sacred Congregation of Propaganda, warmly recommended these works to the Foundress who, after appealing to the houses of the Institute, received so many acceptances from apostolic souls that it did not take much to send numerous groups of sisters to Africa. That was a very happy time for missionary vocations; from 1895 to 1900, thirty to forty sisters left for Africa and America each year; and the Lord of the harvest was inspiring more and more. The clothings of novices continued at a surprising pace, showing the power of grace. This gave the Mother tremendous joy, and she continued courageously to accept new houses. On 20 June 1895, the Villa Cosenza in Naples, today Villa Sant’Anna and the headquarters of the Province, was purchased for the Institute through the generosity of Mgr. Granito di Belmonte.

In October that same year, the General Chapter chaired by Cardinal Verga was also held; Sr. Anna Maria Teresa Patti di Sorrentino was included among the assistants.

The following year (1896), the Institute opened a house for assistance to the sick in Barcelona, Spain.

New claims and provocations of Mother Rosa’s son-in-law ~ This flourishing burst of life was not without storms and conflicts that deeply saddened Mother Rosa, who tried in various ways to lessen their impact. Persons linked to her by kinship, particularly her son-in-law, Gasparo Barbiellini, as has already been mentioned, waged an absurd war on her with blackmail and provocation, claiming presumed rights to property of the Institute. His arrogant claims, his attempts to corrupt the lawyers, all the expedients he used to pursue an unjust end as well as his hypocritical and prevaricating attitudes created deep sorrow for the Mother. All her attempts at a reconciliation were in vain, while calumnies and falsehoods began to tarnish the Institute’s good name and prestige.5 The faithful secretary, Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza says: “Because of this slander, our beloved Mother had to die of sorrow”.6

Even among those anxieties, this extraordinary woman continued on her path of charity, ready to accept the invitations of the Holy See which was asking her to found new works, such as, towards the end of 1897, one in Pernambuco, Brazil. Like the sun setting on a magnificent summer day, the rays of her light seemed to glow more brightly towards the end of her life.

Last journey to Sicily ~ Although she was in a bad way, she made her last journey to Sicily in spring 1898. Her sisters had asked the Cardinal Protector to dissuade her from this effort; but the Cardinal replied: “The sufferings that beset the Mother are not ordinary, so I do not feel like opposing her”.7

She set out on 4 March, and after stopping briefly in Naples, Reggio Calabria and Messina she arrived in Palermo. Here, on 10 April, she gathered all the sisters on the island for a spiritual retreat. Almost forewarned that this might be the last time they saw her, she left them the most heartfelt recommendations of fidelity to their vocation.

“In kissing the crucifix, say: O Lord, I want to be with you until death. Before sleeping: O Lord, give me holy perseverance!”.8

She left Palermo after a month but was unable to complete the visitation of the houses in Sicily because the popular uprisings which broke out that May throughout Italy forced her to hasten back to Rome. Indeed, her brother Francesco came to meet her in Messina, and on 10 May persuaded her to leave without delay. She reached Rome towards the end of the month.

The results of Mother Rosa’s tiring journey then became evident: a great depletion of her strength, difficulty with breathing and an extremely weak heart. The doctor therefore advised her to leave Rome, so she set out for Piacenza where the Feast of St. Anne was celebrated with special solemnity.

Weighing up the achievements of the Mother’s last journey to Sicily, we can indeed describe it as a last triumph. Sr. Anna Celsa, the secretary, writes further: “She was welcomed with transports of joy by all who knew her because her holiness was now famous and clear to everyone”.9

We can truly speak of overflowing enthusiasm in Mother Rosa’s last years, although the other crucifying aspect of her one reality of self-giving should also be considered. These were years of great fruitfulness, but at the same time of great sorrows, borne in deep loneliness.

The serious situation of discontent which had been stirred up in the Institute either because of the spread of calumnious rumors within it (the accusations that the Mother was disposing of the Institute’s property to enrich her relatives have already been mentioned) or because of stormy relations with her son-in-law, who did not fail to have continual recourse to the Roman congregations, finally resulted in the intervention of the Holy See, as has been fully explained.

Although she was motivated by a very great faith and therefore abandoned herself to God’s will with regard to what might result from that visitation, then and in the following months she felt as though she were enveloped in thick darkness; she saw substantially that the ecclesiastical authority had at the very least serious suspicions about the Work’s functioning, and this could not but have caused her deep suffering. Her expression became thoughtful and melancholy, her soul was in anguish as though from one moment to the next a serious sentence were to be pronounced on the Institute she had founded. “Yet”, she sometimes said sighing and as though ending a long discourse that had taken place in her heart, “and yet, in my work my only aim has been the glory of God”.10

Spiritual testament (30 August 1898) ~ On 30 August, her name day, while her spirit was so deeply afflicted, her sisters and the novices of Piacenza wanted to offer her a little celebration. On that occasion she poured into her daughters’ spirits the fullness of her motherly heart, as though she were making her spiritual testament. “Your demonstrations of affection”, she said, “have truly moved me. I first thank the superior who, heedless of effort, has done her utmost with affection to celebrate this day. And I also thank you, beloved daughters; I have always believed in your affection, but especially today, gathered here, you all show me how much you love me. Yes, love the Mother, love her in the holy Church, love her in the Mother St. Anne. I am ashamed that the holy Mother still supports me, still turns her motherly gaze kindly upon me. For in the vastness of this Institute, the mission is great and the circumstances that constantly batter these weak members are many. Physical pain, contradictions, apprehensions, anxieties would have long since made me succumb […].Truly, Daughters, you should not think that all you see that is great in the Institute is due to me; no, you owe it to the Holy Mother. I am only a most unworthy creature […]. A far worthier creature who would have acted better than me should have been chosen to spread this Institute, to direct you who are all angels, all beautiful souls. I am the vilest creature, the most wretched; but the Good Lord and the Holy Mother have turned their gaze on me and in me worked great things. I work, I struggle, but it is all the divine virtue that dwells within me; although I am unworthy, drained of strength, I strive with everything I have for you and will never lose my vocation. Daughters, I want one promise from you today: and it is that you will be faithful to the Institute and to holy Mother Church. No, Daughters, let no slander, trouble, or anxiety, prevent you from following your holy vocation, the sublime grace that you received from God.

I too was slandered, scorned, maltreated: but I never had the slightest worry about my holy vocation. Be strong to withstand all the assaults, fight valiantly and you will be victorious. Always keep in mind the words I am saying to you at this moment, put them in practice and you will be happy. Daughters, when obedience seems too difficult for you, should you be needed in America, in distant lands, obey willingly; prefer a thousand deaths rather than failing in holy obedience […]. Look at the crucified Christ when you are assailed by tribulations; and who suffered more than he? […]. He will be our strength, our guide. He will fight with us and will be our courage […]. I love you all in God, I clasp you to my breast and do all I can to serve you. I do not know what else to say; my thoughts are of God alone, my only support, and no one can take me from him. I love you daughters, but in God, in that immense love that endures in all hearts; be grateful, dear daughters. Pray for me and I will keep you engraved in my heart. God bless you!”.11

Circumstances gave the Mother’s heartfelt speech a mysterious power: her soul’s greatness, her most intense love for Christ, the magnanimity and motherly tenderness of her feelings perhaps never appeared so clearly as at that moment; and it is easy to imagine how deeply moved the community listening to her must have been.

Deterioration of health ~ Meanwhile the Mother’s health, so undermined, soon deteriorated; she therefore sought a remedy by staying for a while at the villa in Quercione near Piacenza, but it was all in vain. So she wished to return to Piacenza. As autumn approached, she asked the Visitor if she could go to Naples, where important matters awaited her; in the meantime she would stop in Piacenza until the first fortnight of November. The Visitor agreed and that stay in Piacenza slightly benefited the health of the Mother who was now thoroughly worn out.

These were the last days of her life in Piacenza. She spent many hours in her cell, tasting the pain of the latest events and ever clinging to her crucified Christ. There she had seen the first shoots of the Institute, she had tended them and strengthened them with her tears, her prayers and her penances. What ineffable secrets her Good had revealed to her within those poor walls! What delights had flooded her spirit! So she meditated once again in that absolute solitude as she felt the threatening onslaught of the tempest while the tree of the Institute, now gigantic, seemed caught up and tossed by the whirlwind. Like her crucified Good, she generously accepted the bitterest cup during the last days of her life. And then she felt new strength flowering in her soul to take up the last challenge of hope.

Last reminder to the novices and definitive departure from Piacenza ~ Shortly after mid-October she gathered the novices of the Mother House around her and gave them a stirring talk on various spiritual topics, and obviously the love of God did not come last. “For some time I have wanted to be with you”, she said, “and I should have left unwillingly and with great sorrow if I had not come to give you something by which to remember me. I leave you a reminder, O beloved Daughters: love of God […]; not a languid love, but love, true love. A difficult word to understand; not a cold, sterile love, but the true love that a bride of Jesus Christ must possess. St. Teresa said: ‘Whoever loves does not offend the beloved’”.

Then going into detail, she insisted heavily on fidelity to meditation and on the way to meditate, because without this one does not grow in love of God. She sculpted in these words the importance of this religious practice, which is the source of all spirituality in those who are striving for perfection: “You are in the novitiate to learn how to meditate well”. And here, as a true spiritual teacher and citing St. Teresa, she made those young girls realize that without space for contemplation there can be no firmness of virtue.

Therefore, returning to love of God, she revealed the obstacles to the fullness of love in her incisive style which customarily touched on the needs of the soul: “A religious must always think of Jesus, love him and be all his […]. How beautiful it is to be wholly detached from relatives, from superiors, from that sick person, from the confessor! […] Love God and you will be happy”, the great Mother concluded, “and may God bless you”12. Those novices gathered up the notes of the talk and treasured them; it was their Foundress’s last viaticum for undertaking the arduous ascent towards holiness.

On 18 October 1898 Mother Rosa, having carefully closed her very poor room, left Piacenza for ever, leaving those Daughters of hers in the deepest desolation. She stayed only a few days in Rome, then went to Naples, where she remained for a month, putting in order the serious matters of government that had required her presence. On 28 December she was back in Rome.

The balance of that much-troubled year turned out to be wonderful: fourteen new houses opened, six clothings of novices in the Generalate alone and several more in the other novitiate houses. Thus the words of the psalmist came true: “Those who sow in tears will reap with songs of joy” (Ps 126:5).

Feast of St. Anne in Rome ~ In 1899, while more and more preparations were being made to celebrate the end of the century, tireless Mother Rosa did several things that aroused astonishment, since it was impossible to see clearly what sentiments prompted them. First she wanted the Generalate to be redecorated from top to bottom, inside and out, for which a large team of plasterers and painters turned various floors of the house upside down over a long period. Perhaps disturbed by the bustle, one of the sisters in the Mother’s confidence asked the Mother why she was having this work done, and if she was expecting someone important.

“Well, really”, she replied, “a little sprucing up was necessary!”. In fact, there were no extraordinary visits that year, but this way of acting had all the features of expectation and preparation for something important; some sisters in fact, said they guessed that the Mother had foreseen her forthcoming departure from this world.1

She wanted the Feast of St. Anne more solemnly celebrated than ever; unsatisfied with the tapestries brought by the decorator to adorn the church, she wanted others. As well as the many lamps already hung in the Roman tradition around the altar and down the nave, she wanted another one which was customarily used in St. Mary Major, which it was almost impossible to get into the Church of Mater Gratiae, since the doorway was not wide enough. Many of the workmen wondered what event that year might justify such pomp.

During the triduum of the feast, she managed to arrange for the Eucharistic blessing to be imparted every evening by the most eminent Cardinals, and indeed Cardinal Satolli, Cardinal Cretoni and Cardinal Parocchi, Vicar of Rome of His Holiness Leo XIII, all came. On the evening of the feast, the Parish Committee of San Martino ai Monti also took part. The general Communion administered by Cardinal Satolli was so widely attended that the great quantity of consecrated wafers did not suffice. In brief, it was a real triumph for the great Patroness of the Institute; and the Mother was exultant, for she had wanted the celebration to be a special tribute to St. Anne for the countless graces obtained in 33 years; she had felt inspired by the saint to organize that solemnity and confided to a sister: “I think that the Holy Mother wanted this thanksgiving celebration from me, perhaps because it is the last one I shall celebrate on this earth”.2

Deterioriation of health and stay in Liguria ~ In fact, the alarming signs of the illness that was finally to bring her to the grave were soon manifest. The excessive heat of the season and the increasing swelling further undermined her strength which was already so depleted; she found it difficult and painful to move, nor could she remain standing for even a moment without suffering; her breathing had become really labored, to the point that she was forced to leave Rome as soon as possible.

The General Council would have liked her to go to Tuscany, where on previous occasions she had considerably benefited, but she preferred Liguria because she had not been there for some time and thought she could do a little good to those houses of the Institute, combining her visit with her recuperation. In fact, she left on 31 July for Ovada, stopping for two days in Pisa where her brother Francesco came to meet her. For the rest of the journey, which she did by night, she suffered badly, finding it so difficult to breathe that the sisters accompanying her and her brother were sick with worry. When she finally reached Ovada she was taken into the hospice of Lercaro.

After a temporary improvement which lasted for a few days, the Mother went into a visible decline: she could not eat, had very bad headaches, restless nights and insomnia. On 20 August the sick woman was taken to Sestri Ponente, in the hope that the house, more comfortable and spacious, and the sea air might do her good; but it made no difference and on 31 August it was decided to make a further change and move her to Sampierdarena. Here it seemed at last that the Mother was recovering some of her strength; she became, or at least tried to be more cheerful with the sisters around her, to the point that it seemed as though the illness tormenting her were less serious. She stayed in Sampierdarena almost a month.

At the end of September she went to Genoa, to the house of San Silvestro, and seemed so strong that she was allowed to walk up the hill supported by her sisters. However, increased swelling and difficulty in breathing soon showed that her illness was about to get the upper hand.

On 12 October, an unexpected crisis seemed to indicate the end; the doctor feared a heart attack. The Mother continued in that state from the evening until two o’clock in the afternoon on the following day: her condition then improved slightly, as the doctor, Prof. Lupi, also recorded. Consequently, two days later the decision was made to take her to Rome.

Return to Rome ~ She left on 15 October in the evening, settled on the train, accompanied by several sisters and her brother, Francesco; Prof. Lupi assisted her, and dosed her little by little with the medicines she needed to overcome the crisis.

As soon as she arrived in Rome, there was an immediate consultation between Prof. Lupi and Dr. Montechiari, who renewed the general hope of seeing Mother Rosa soon restored to health, as in fact happened; so that in November and December, she somehow managed to deal with various important matters of the Institute. Among other things, she took care to write a clear will all in her own hand, to prevent any problems regarding the patrimony of the Institute; but she also found a way to express in it the deep sentiments of her soul, always marked by Christian faith. “At the foot of my beloved crucified Christ”, she said in it, “I beg my dear Daughters of St. Anne not to worry about my funeral and the transportation of my body, but to do only what our Constitutions prescribe […]. I would like to forgive anyone who might even involuntarily have offended me and caused damage, as I likewise ask forgiveness of everyone. I bless my daughter, my son-in-law and their children, my grandchildren, imploring God for every good. I also desire for my brothers, Federico and Francesco, and my sisters, Giusta and Elisa, every good on this earth and in eternal life”. The document is dated 20 November 1899.3

Episcopal consecration of Mgr. Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte ~ On 26 of the same month, the Mother had the immense consolation of seeing the great friend and benefactor of the Daughters of St. Anne, Mgr. Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, consecrated bishop in the Church of Maria Mater Gratiae. He was immediately appointed Apostolic Nuncio in Brussels. Cardinal Rampolla, Secretary of State, presided at the ceremony and indeed on this occasion accepted to be the Institute’s new protector, since Cardinal Verga had recently died. These events gave the Mother deep joy, and she was also particularly pleased with the appointment of the new Protector, although this step had worried the Apostolic Visitor who feared some “coup de main” that might put an end to the current Visitation (cf. Summ. Doc. p. 814 and pp. 823-825).

The news was also spreading at the time that the Supreme Pontiff Leo XIII had indicted the Holy Year for the end of the 19th century and that the ceremony of the opening of the Holy Door was to take place on Christmas Eve. The rite had not been celebrated for 75 years, so the whole world was exultant. This event was a new cause of joy to Mother Gattorno, whose immediate thought was how to put the Generalate at the disposal of the bishops and prelates who would be coming to Rome.

God’s plans for her, however, were rather different.

Last letters written by the Mother ~ The Mother, as in previous years, at Christmas 1899 inserted many images of the Infant Jesus in her letters of good wishes to the sisters. In one them, these words are written in her hand: “Jesus, consume me with your love! I will be eternally happy”. The fortunate sisters who received these keepsakes kept them jealously, writing on them the date and a few affectionate words. We interpret it as Mother Rosa’s passionate preparation for her great, definitive encounter with her Good.

On 10 February 1900, she succumbed to a serious attack of influenza and did not recover. Her heart condition so deteriorated that the catastrophe was foreseen.

Dr. Montechiari, who had been caring for the sick woman for some time, declared that for about twelve years she had been affected with interstitial nephritis, and had been subject to attacks of cardiac arrhythmia for about a year, due to arteriosclerosis. In such critical conditions the Mother never wanted to be touched anywhere above her pulse; she so jealously concealed the signs of her life of penance that in all her illnesses she never let a doctor examine her and even refused Prof. Marchiafava, although the distinguished man had given her a respectful reprimand. We know, in fact, that for many years she had worn a heavy chain around her waist.

In the meantime, long prayers were said by day and night at the Generalate and throughout the Institute.

Because of the swelling which had spread all over her body, the sick Mother could not remain in bed; she therefore spent most of the day sitting on a chair, but constantly refused any kind of comfortable armchair. She became drowsy easily but as soon as she opened her eyes she would turn them to the crucifix she kept by her on the table; then she would begin to write letters to the distant sisters, as she had done all her life, and wanted to the very last to treat them with this motherly love. Two letters which the Mother wrote to two superiors of America (Potosì and Lima) were found in the folder on her writing table. The writing is almost illegible but one can clearly distinguish the Mother’s keen desire still to be ever present for her distant daughters. “…I write badly […] pray for me […] believe me yours in my dear crucified Christ”.

These were perhaps her last words, written with an extreme effort. One of her last letters was dictated, as has been said, six days before her death, because it was henceforth absolutely impossible for her to write.

Visit from Cardinal Rampolla ~ Cardinal Rampolla came to visit her on 18 April; he was invited by the Mother herself in a note dictated to Sr. Anna Celsa which said: “I dare to request Your Eminence for a visit, since I need your lofty advice. The Lord’s Work is flourishing, although it has been battered by small squalls which came to upset it to make it ever more beautiful in the gracious progress of the Church through all the centuries […]. Oh, God’s work was born in obedience, fear, crosses and sufferings: that is the origin of the Work of the Lord”.4

The Cardinal talked to her, comforting her and promising her that that very evening he would obtain a special blessing for her from the Holy Father. Then speaking of the Institute, he expressed some fears about the future that it might have, since rumors were already spreading about greedy claims for some of the property of the Congregation she had founded. The Mother replied calmly, reassuring the Protector and affirming that “the Institute was like an indestructible rock, and that after her death there would be no difficulties for the person who would have to govern it”.5

On 25 April she had another heart attack; Prof. Marchiafava, summoned urgently, declared that her condition was very serious and her death at hand. The sisters who had been close to her in the activity of her long governance clustered more closely around her than ever; her most affectionate Secretary, Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza seemed more upset than the others, so the Mother expressed the desire to be alone with her for a while for an intimate talk. She again repeated to her the clearest reassurances about the Daughters of St. Anne and said: “After my death my relatives will not be able to do anything, and Sr. Anna del Salvatore6 will be at the gate […]. The Institute will have a time of peace and tranquillity after my death, because I am the obstacle and cause of all this strife”.

What humility and trust in a soul that was so great! Until Wednesday, 2 May the Mother had never stayed in bed all the time; she would eat a little food in her study and in the afternoon of that day she could still enter the office to visit her sisters at work. But at about one o’clock in the afternoon Thursday, 3 May, she suffered another heart attack, with vomiting and fainting; she was now near her end. In fact, according to the doctors, she had developed violent entero-peritonitis, largely due to the ingestion of indigestible substances.7

On 2 May, since she had become so badly swollen, the Mother herself called her loyal Sr. Anna Serafina, who because of her simplicity and candor was very close to her and had been present during her long hours of prayer; so this sister, who had been with her every night for three months, helped her remove the chain she had worn round her hips for 42 years without once taking it off. Since she could not open it because the clasp had been locked, Sr. Anna Serafina had to lay hands on some strong pliers and break another link; in removing the chain, obviously some shreds of flesh caught up in it were torn away, because it been bound so tightly round her for so long, and because of the recent swelling8.

When the news of the irreparable deterioration of the Foundress’ health spread to the houses of Rome and the surroundings, there was an immediate flow of religious to her bedside. At midday on Friday, 4 May, the Mother told those who surrounded her: “Now I have finished suffering: everything has been averted!”. And she meant that she considered the ominous shadows which had obscured the Institute’s splendor in recent times had been dispelled for ever.

The image of Maria Mater Gratiae ~ Towards evening on the same day, she expressed her desire to have brought to her room the image of “Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae” which was in the house chapel and had belonged to Fr. Bernardo M. Clausi. It was brought there with its own small stand and she wanted the candles lit. Then getting out of the rather low bed without help, standing with difficulty and supported, she stood in prayer before the beloved image for about 10 minutes. At a hint from her, the sisters had withdrawn and were just outside the door where they stood in silence wondering, and not daring to do anything.

When she was back in bed, the sisters again crowded round her and she gave them orders to prepare everything for the Holy Viaticum which she wished to receive that very evening. She had received Communion every day, even during her long and painful illness, sometimes without fasting beforehand or immediately after midnight, in accordance with the faculties granted by Leo XIII; yet she insisted on receiving the great gift of Christ’s body that very evening from the hands of Fr. Agostino Donadio of the Minims. Her insistence was providential, since it was her last Communion; the next day she was prostrate and vomited so frequently that she could no longer swallow anything. After Saturday morning she had such difficulty speaking that no one could understand her, not even her brother Francesco who had come to visit her. However, she continued to be perfectly lucid and tenderly stretched out her hands and gazed at the image of Maria Mater Gratiae which she had had set up at the foot of her bed.

Death of Mother Rosa (6 May 1900) ~ Although she was declining and her death was imminent, on the evening of that Saturday, the eve of the last day of her life, she was still determined with incredible strength to get out of bed, as on the previous day, to pray for a few moments before the image of Our Lady. Fr. Donadio, who was also there, was deeply moved by this; some sisters would have liked to prevent her from making the effort, but others did not want to deny the Mother this last and most tender act, prompted by deep filial affection for the Mother of God. Who knows what inexpressible emotions and feelings must have filled that last prayer! “Now I won’t get out of bed any more”, she stammered, returning to lie down. And these were her only distinct words that Saturday.

Towards nine o’clock in the evening she was invited to receive the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick; with gestures, she made it plain that she was very glad to receive it and tried to articulate two words which to those around her sounded like: “Così sia” [So may it be]. In any case this was her last sentence in this world. The sacrament was administered to her by Fr. Vincenzo da Alatri, a Capuchin, who was her confessor and the community’s confessor, and he imparted the Apostolic Blessing to her. Then she entered her agony.

The next morning, Sunday, 6 May 1900, during the festivities for the anniversary of the dedication of the Church of Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae (in fact, celebrated on the first Sunday in May), outside in Via Merulana, as groups of pilgrims were passing on their way to St Mary Major and St John Lateran, Mother Rosa gave up her soul to God at nine o’clock, in perfect abandonment and tranquillity. Present were Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, Sr. Anna Amante La Barbera on whose lap the dying woman had rested her hands, Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia and a few other sisters.

In carrying out the last services for the beloved body and dressing it in the religious habit, Sr. Anna Serafina and the sisters helping her came across various old scars on the upper part of her body; they also saw traces of other wounds on the forearms and shoulders. Around her waist, apart from the lacerations caused by the iron chain which had been removed three days earlier, they noted an area of scars about 15 or 18 centimeters long, caused by the bodice with iron points which she had frequently worn. On the left side of her breast, Sr. Anna Serafina saw a rather deep scar, about five centimeters long and large enough to put a finger in; the edges were violet-colored. Without a doubt this scar had been caused by the small crucifix which she had bound to her breast in early widowhood and had worn for more than five years until it became embedded in her flesh. The Mother had removed it through obedience, as was told in Chapter III. In her writings, she often mentions a wound in the area of her heart which tormented her; it is likely to have been this. In any case, all these scars were a clear proof, the trophy of a glorious battle fought for more than 40 years, of a passionate, explosive love for the crucified Christ.

Here it should be recalled that the Mother had made Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia and other sisters helping her promise that even in case of extreme need they would never allow any man to touch her, not even after her death. This is the reason why Rome: interior of the church after the alterations of 1925-27 they did not accept her brother Federico’s offer to inject her dead body to preserve it from corruption.9

The Daughters’ tribute of affection; funeral and transportation of her body to Verano ~ Hundreds of sisters shortly arrived to pay their last tribute of affection to their beloved Mother. In the afternoon several religious, having heard of the scar in her side, asked to see it; but because of the rapid decomposition of the venerable body, it was impossible to proceed after the first attempts at removing the clothes.

The Mother’s corpse was arranged on the bed in the room in which she had died, and there it remained until the afternoon of the following day. It was then placed in a double case of wood and lead and on Monday evening moved to the chapel in the Generalate. On Tuesday morning, 8 May, the Feast of the Apparition of St. Michael Archangel for whom the Mother had had a special devotion, the case was enclosed in a walnut coffin and taken into the church of the Daughters of St. Anne for the funeral rite. Streams of people, including numerous members of the Roman aristocracy, came to participate in the many Masses that were celebrated.

In the afternoon it was transported to Campo Verano; the coffin was accompanied by more than 200 Daughters of St. Anne, the two Associations of the Daughters of Mary, many Capuchins and a long line of the common people.

The body was temporarily laid in the common tomb of the Daughters of St. Anne in Verano; after a year, since in the meantime the mortuary chapel of the Institute had been built, it was removed and taken there, set above the entrance in a sarcophagus of marble, the front of which was decorated with a beautiful sculpture of the Mother’s face. It immediately became a destination of pilgrimage for every Daughter of St. Anne who came through Rome, and for many people who had been fond of Mother Rosa or who desired to obtain graces through her intercession.

Exhumation and transportation of her body to the church of the Generalate (1932) ~ After 32 years, the Mother General, Sr. Anna Corredentrice Pomarici, obtained permission from the ecclesiastical authority to transfer the Foundress’ body to the Church of the Institute in Via Merulana. In the morning of 6 February 1932, the members of the ecclesiastical Tribune of the Vicariate of Rome, various prelates and a numerous crowd of Daughters of St. Anne headed by their Mother General and her Council all met at Verano.

In accordance with canonical procedures, the tomb was opened and the heavy coffin taken out and carried in procession to lie in the observation room.

The following Monday, 8 February, they returned to Verano where the ecclesiastical Tribunal and the sisters were joined by Mother Rosa’s youngest grandchild, Count Bernardo Barbiellini Amidei, Dr. Simpa, appointed by the Vicariate, and Dr. Vivaldi, by the Department of Public Health. When the coffin was opened a thick gray layer of mold appeared on a mass of putrefying cloth. Dr. Vivaldi immediately ordered the coffin to be closed, for he thought that the body must be in a process of putrefaction, but Dr. Simpa insisted that an official, if perfunctory, act of recognition be made.

Two serving men then lifted a strip of the cloth from the head, and lo and behold, the Mother’s sweet face appeared; it was turned to the left, serene, dry, a little brown but intact. Her mouth was slightly open almost as if she were breathing, and the right eye was also half open. Lifting away other strips of that layer of decomposed cloth, the whole body could be clearly seen to be incorrupt. It was then thoroughly cleansed with formaline. As it was gradually cleansed, the flesh became whiter and it was still soft to the touch.

Her grandson was granted to cleanse the face; he wiped the cheeks and forehead with affectionate care, lowered the eyelids, set the lips, soft and intact like those of a sleeping person. Her soft hair, firmly attached to the scalp, looked shiny and beautiful, as though freshly brushed. Many of the sisters present could clearly see the scar on her breast left by the crucifix.

The following day, 9 February, three religious finished recomposing the body; they wrapped it in a sheet of very fine linen and dressed it in a new religious habit, noting with surprise the great flexibility of the arms and a certain softness of the flesh. Having then lain it in the new coffin, arranging the head on a white satin cushion, they took a photograph of her, desiring to have incontestable proof of this surprising event. A cylindrical box containing the parchment of the attestation signed by the members of the ecclesiastical Tribunal and by the Mother General Pomarici was also placed in the coffin.

Finally, having closed the double coffin of zinc and wood, it was sealed with the seals of the Vicariate and taken to the cemetery chapel where it remained for four months.

On the evening of 14 June, the Foundress’ body was taken back to the House in Via Merulana, where the Daughters of St. Anne, deeply moved, received the mortal remains of their very great Mother. The following day a solemn funeral commemoration was held, attended by many distinguished clerical and lay figures of Rome.

At Vespers that same day, in the presence of Cardinal di Belmonte, Mother Rosa’s body was laid to rest in a beautiful marble monument under the nave of the Church of Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae, by the main altar.10

Second exhumation (1981) ~ Later, in 1960 it was entombed in a more visible burial niche, and in 1981 it was re-exhumed and canonically recognized in order to proceed to its translation in the same public church.

In the presence of Mgr. Petti, Promotor of the faith, of Mgr. Cocchetti, Chancellor of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, of the Postulator Fr. Cairoli, of the Superior General Sr. Anna Elda Bernasconi and of several sisters, the double coffin was opened and the Mother’s body was once again discovered to be intact, in a state of mummification. After treating the body with preservatives and re-clothing it in a new religious habit, it was enclosed in a triple coffin. The coffin was carried to the sisters’ church privately and after the solemn concelebration at which Cardinal Poletti, Vicar of His Holiness presided, it was replaced in the sarcophagus, while hymns from the Liturgy of the Dead were sung11.

In 1912 it had been decided to introduce Mother Rosa’s Cause of beatification, and on 1 January that year, Mother Benedetta Carrega had Fr. Francesco Vittozzi appointed Postulator.

On 27 July 1912 the ordinary informative process on the fame of her holiness, her life, her virtues and her miracles began. This lengthy process lasted for at least 15 years, and occupied 444 sessions, closing on 26 January 1927.

Other informative processes were held in the meantime in Genoa, Piacenza, Naples and Palermo; the documentation as a whole amounts to the considerable bulk of almost 8,000 foolscap pages. In 1979, once the delay that had held it up for over 40 years had been removed, the Cause received new impetus, and in 1991 the Positio super virtutibus, edited by the Postulator Fr. Carlos Lizarraga, C.P., was printed.

The Institute rooted in Rosa Gattorno’s heart ~ Over many years much has been said about wonderful graces obtained from God through Mother Rosa’s intercession, and several are recounted in the processes mentioned above; some have even been supported by sworn testimony, but it would be impossible to relate them, both because they would form an almost endless series and because of the due discretion required by the ecclesiastical authority, which has not yet pronounced its judgment on those facts.

One event, however, we cannot and must not pass over in silence: it is the living fruit of Mother Rosa’s work.

Jesus said that a tree is known by its fruits; well, the work founded by this generous woman clearly bears the seal of God, who inspired and sustained it. At her death it was already imposing, as we saw in Chapter XIII; in the years that followed those figures increased considerably, bearing witness to the constant flourishing of the Institute.

This luxuriant tree, ever shaken by the renewing wind of the Spirit, ever fruitful because constantly open to the challenges of hope, sinks its roots in the immense heart of Rosa Gattorno, still and always a “mother” with a most tender, self-giving embrace. Her life, extraordinarily rich in mystical gifts and at the same time in overflowing humanity, has been and remains a message that becomes light, a witness to the highest spiritual values, valid more than ever in our own time. Mother Rosa knew how to look further, to read the signs of hope in an age marked by darkness and bewilderment; she said her heroic and conscious “yes” to God and to history, and she undoubtedly wrote an exalting chapter of that history.

Draft of the above-mentioned letter to Archbishop Charvaz

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

The last time that I had the grace to be in your presence to speak to you, you ordered me to put down in writing those observations of what it would be necessary to modify in the Rule of the Ursulines. Now, although I am capable of nothing, with God’s help I obey your command.

I am not returning to those articles of the Rule on which Your Most Reverend Excellency has already made your observations, such as n. 47, which speaks of confessors, and article 13, which speaks of the vow of chastity. Having removed these, in my opinion, it would also be appropriate to remove n. 15. It also seems to me that Superiors are required who have great energy and knowledge, and who can do more than genteel ladies’ work, which it seems to me will be very difficult, especially as they must live in the world.

Your Most Reverend Excellency also commanded me to explain whether something had been introduced into the Society which was not in the Rule, and mentioned to me the confession of faults made by the Daughters at their meetings in the presence of the Superior. I would be of the opinion that these confessions should be left as they are, and indeed I would deem it necessary, so that the members remember to practize those observances which are contained in the Rule, otherwise I am sure that few would do so; I really intend that this confession of faults should always be in the Rule.

This is what my lowliness has permitted me to observe. With regard to other uses or abuses, it seems to me that it is not my business to mention them, but when there is a Superior and a Superior General appointed by Your Most Reverend Excellency, they will be able, having more faculties, to remove any use or abuse, and to see that everything proceeds well.

In the meantime, I take this opportunity to reveal to you what the Lord commands me, and I hope that in so doing I will not disappoint you, and that Your Most Reverend Excellency will give me your holy approval and in addition, make whatever observations that you may deem appropriate since I am too wretched a creature and capable of nothing and too weak an instrument; and that they will be quite right, so that the Lord’s works will be more and more resplendent, and thus nothing will be attributed to us.

It is a question of founding a Conservatorio of Daughters entitled Daughters of Mary Immaculate, Minims of St. Francis of Assisi. They will also admit widows who desire to become Religious even if some have wretched health. These Religious will care for persons of their own sex who are seriously ill at home: they will also take in young girls in danger. In addition, they will observe perfect obedience and poverty: they will work for the poor and for the poor Churches. They will take an annual vow of chastity until a certain age, when they will also be able to make their perpetual profession.

Human beings continue to destroy, and the Lord builds, constructing stronger walls.

I hope that Your Most Reverend Excellency will forgive me; I beg you to believe that what I have done has caused me great suffering. I trust totally in you as, prostrate at your feet, I request your Holy Blessing,

Your Humble and Obedient Servant,

ROSA GATTORNO, Widow of GEROLAMO CUS-TO.

I thank Your Reverence for the present copy which you have been pleased to make me of the Rule which is to serve for the Sodality of the Daughters of St. Anne established by you. If there is anything that might by chance require to be further perfected in the said Rule it will be more evident through practice and experience.

Reverend Madam, as I impart my pastoral blessing to you and to the daughters associated with you, I extend my respectful esteem to you.

LETTER FROM MGR. MARIANO WANSTIENKIST to Mother Gattorno, announcing the condemnation of the Rule written by Fr. Tornatore (AFSA B.2.72).

Most Reverend Mother Superior,

The Most Reverend Mother will certainly have been informed through this Curia of Piacenza of the measure issued by the Holy See through the Sacred Congregation for Bishops and Regulars concerning the request for approval of the Rule of your Institute, that is, since the Rule cannot be admitted in its form or substance as it has been compiled, all copies of it, both the booklet entitled PAROLE DELLA GLORIOSA S. ANNA MADRE DELL’IMMACOLATA CHE PRESENTA LE REGOLE ALLE SUE FIGLIE (Words of the Glorious St. Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate in presenting the Rule to her daughters) and the second one, APPLICAZIONE DELLA REGOLA COMMUNE ALLE SORELLE INFERMIERE (Application of the common Rule to the nursing sisters) must be withdrawn by the Ecclesiastical Authorities from whoever may be in possession of them, and the above mentioned printed copies destroyed. The Sacred Congregation also orders the Author of the said works, whoever he may be, and the assistants and propagators of the same, to be removed and banned from being present in or directing the said Institute in any capacity. With regard to [what] concerns the House in Ferrara, without alarming your good and virtuous Daughters, you should write to the Superior that she herself should withdraw all copies of it and give them to Monsignor Vicar General, since in conscience she cannot refuse this authoritative provision of the Holy See.

Most esteemed Mother, you should not be at all discouraged by this result, since if the Supreme Authority of the Church cannot accept the form and substance of the Rule as it has been presented, and proibisce (prohibits) [sic: perhaps prescrivere] (prescribes) that the persons who had any part in it be banned, this does not mean that an Institute which has already offered and will be able to offer great spiritual and temporal comforts to others should not exist. Therefore take heart, since it is right that you should put to the test the lovely virtues which adorn you, as it is well known that the more gold is purified in the crucible and polished, the shinier and more precious it becomes.

You should let me have the following information as soon as possible: 1. The origins of the Pious Institute, and the goal it has set for itself. 2. The number of Women of which it is currently composed, and the number of houses into which it is now divided; you should mention the places and the activities of each House. 3. The spirit and discipline with which it is imbued. 4. The financial means of its support, and any other relevant information.

Then I would advise you to write a letter of humble submission and obedience to what the Holy See has ordered, that the Institute is ready to vivere (live) sic: perhaps ricevere any other measure, and to observe the Rule with that title with which it is desired to call the Institute, which was enjoined, having no other aim than the Greater Glory of God and the spiritual and temporal wellbeing of others.

Your most humble, devoted and obedient Servant MARIANO WANSTIENKIST Rome, 17 February 1872.

LETTER from Bishop Antonio Ranza to the Prefect of the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars in which he informs him that he has carried out the orders concerning the 1869 Rule, and further praises the Foundress and the Institute (Arch. Congr. per i Religiosi P 31, photocopy in AFSA C.3.161).

Your Most Reverend Eminence,

The orders, which on the part of this Sacred Congregation Your Most Reverend Eminence was pleased to give me with your venerable letter of 7 February last, did not arrive until the third day of this current month of March. It was appropriate for me to say this first to show that the delay in their execution was not my fault, since I am ever willing to be a prompt and faithful executor of any measures I receive from the Holy Apostolic See.

Therefore having received the above mentioned venerable orders, I immediately arranged to withdraw all the copies of the two works: THE WORDS OF THE GLORIOUS ST. ANNE, MOTHER OF MARY IM-

THE RULE MACULATE

IN

PRESENTING

TO

HER DAUGHTERS, AND APPLICATIONS OF THE COMMON RULE TO THE NURSING SISTERS.

By good fortune I was able to see them brought to me immediately in four large sealed bundles, because since Mrs. Rosa Gattorno learned before me of this measure she had gathered up and called for all the copies of the above-mentioned works, not only from the two Houses in this City, but likewise from the other Houses in the Archdiocese of Genoa, from the one in Ferrara and from that of Nizza Monferrato, in the Diocese of Acqui. Knowing moreover that they had been printed exclusively for the new Institute, I also had myself informed of the outside people who were in possession of a few copies and I was easily able to withdraw these too, since they had been given only to a very few and prudent Ecclesiastics, who moreover were neither supporters nor propagators of it. Having been given them, I burned them all.

Then the author of the said works at the first hint of the order issued by this Sacred Congregation had kept away from the Houses of the Institute mentioned, and invited to present himself to me, declared to me that he never wanted to set foot there again and will abstain from any interference; in addition he gave me the copy which he had of the two works, together with another four which he had acquired.

As far as I can see, there are no supporters or propagators of these works, as is also evident from what has been mentioned.

Already with my respectful letter of 26 May 1871, with which I took the step of commending to your Most Reverend Eminence’s kindness Mrs. Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Institute known as the Daughters of St. Anne, which until now is only a private association, I informed you that this same lady came here to Genoa to found it towards the middle of 1866. At the beginning she wished to call it the “Institute of Minims of St. Francis of Assisi” but soon, filled with enthusiasm for the devotion to St. Anne, she conceived of the title: THE DAUGHTERS OF ST. ANNE, whom she has chosen as its special protectress and titular.

However, the aim established from the start was barely changed but only expanded, with regard to works of mercy.

The goal that the young and pious women gathered in it under the direction of the same Mrs. Gattorno have chosen for themselves is to attain, through the practice of the Evangelical Counsels, their sanctification, and that of their neighbor through the exercise of works of mercy, both by caring for and educating poor orphan or abandoned girls and those at risk, and by assisting sick persons of both sexes in their own homes, but taking several precautions according to the person’s sex.

I have already noted above, that the number of houses of this Institution amounts to six: there are two in this city of Piacenza, two in the Archdiocese of Genoa, one in the city of Ferrara and one in Nizza Monferrato, in the Diocese of Acqui.

In the first house of Piacenza there are 27 Religious and 65 little girls, only seven of whom are paid for; in 1871 they gave home care to 131 sick persons, all with the approval of their parish priest. In the second house there are 17 Religious; there they run a school for small children of whom there are 88 living in their respective families; and there they assisted 104 persons afflicted with smallpox, again with the approval of their parish priest.

Having acquired the information, I add the number of Daughters of St. Anne who are in Houses outside the diocese at the present time.

In that at Sampierdarena, in the Archdiocese of Genoa there are 18 religious and 40 girls, only eight of whom pay their board.

In the house at Genoa, there are 17 religious; they have a school for 25 children.

In the house at Ferrara, there are 12 religious: and 120 girls.

In the house at Nizza Monferrato in the Diocese of Acqui, there are 10 religious: there is a state school for girls; the state hospital annexed, and the care of girls in danger.

I limit myself, as I must, to speaking of the spirit and discipline with which the religious in the two houses in my Diocese are formed, I cannot but confirm what I submitted to Your Most Reverend Eminence in my above-mentioned letter of 26 May 1871. And to reaffirm my opinion about their spirit of piety, sacrifice and self-denial I have had further certain and more abundant evidence. In fact, although they nursed so many sick people at home there was not the slightest complaint about even one of them: and the whole city admired their self-denial and promptness; thus at the request of individual families and parish priests they went to help those smitten with smallpox, and the city was so edified by them that even sad people show them respect, not daring to contradict the common opinion. As it were to crown this, may I add that at the request of the Prioress, two went to the Monastery of Teresian Religious of Parma where there was great distress; some of the community had contracted smallpox which had killed some of them and the others were either powerless to do anything or discouraged. They devoted such assiduous care to the assistance of the sick that the entire religious family gave them the highest praise for their virtues and self-denial.

In addition to this the Daughters of St. Anne, directed by prudent and zealous Ecclesiastics, have a spirit of docility and obedience to the Authority of the Church, as is proven by the most recent event of their prompt delivery of all the copies of the abovementioned works.

With regard to their financial means, it should be noted that the Institute has no civil possessions, and cannot even possess any in this regard. Whatever the Foundress may possess, either for herself or for the Institute, I am not given to know since she is far from here. I have asked this Superior and she answered me that divine Providence has not let them lack what they need, although so many people live in their communities.

After this it only remains for me to await further orders, which Your Most Reverend Eminence may esteem right to let me know on this subject.

As I bend to kiss the hem of the Sacred Purple, I have the honor to declare myself with perfect esteem and full submission,

Your Most Reverend Eminence’s

Most Humble, Devoted and Indebted Servant,

  • Antonio Bishop of Piacenza
